UNIT.subject: General Science
UNIT.content:
• Alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases and transition metals
• Physical and chemical properties of selected elements
• Uses of the elements and their compounds
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify chemical families in the periodic table,
b) classify elements of the periodic table into their chemical families,
c) investigate the physical and chemical properties of selected elements of the periodic table,
d) outline the uses of elements of the periodic table,
e) appreciate the uses of the elements of the periodic table in day-to-day life.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Self-efficacy: as the learner carries out activities to investigate the reaction of sodium, magnesium and chlorine with air and dilute acids.
• Digital literacy: as the learner uses available digital and print media to research on transition elements and their uses.
UNIT.values: • Love: as the learner takes care of self and others by observing safety when carrying out activities to investigate properties of elements of the periodic table and appropriately using first aid kits in case of injuries.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: learners generate questions on why some elements are used for particular tasks, such as why a jiko sufuria is made of aluminium but wiring of copper, and add them to the Driving Question Board.
• Planning and carrying out investigations: learners test physical properties (conductivity, appearance, hardness) of metals and observe reactions of Group 1 and 2 elements with air, water and dilute acids, using teacher demonstrations for the hazardous ones.
• Analyzing and interpreting data: learners identify patterns in reactivity down a group and across families from observation tables.
• Developing and using models: learners build and revise a family-trends model of the periodic table, linking electron arrangement to reactivity.
• Constructing explanations: learners explain why an element is suited to a use, citing evidence from its properties.
• Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information: learners research transition elements and noble gas uses from digital and print sources and present in plenary.
UNIT.pcis: • Road safety: as the learner discusses with peers the properties of elements that make them suitable for use in illuminating roads.
UNIT.careers:
• Chemist / laboratory technician: investigating and testing the properties of elements and compounds.
• Materials and metallurgical engineer: selecting metals such as copper, iron, zinc and lead for particular uses, for instance in Nairobi's Industrial Area workshops.
• Electrician: choosing copper for wiring and understanding properties of metals.
• Lighting and road engineer: using noble gases for street and highway lighting.
• Water treatment officer: using chlorine to disinfect water, e.g. in Nairobi and Mombasa water works.
• Jua kali metalworker: working with aluminium, iron and zinc (galvanised iron sheets) to make sufurias and mabati roofing.
UNIT.focus: This unit anchors learning in everyday Kenyan objects made from different elements. Learners sort elements into families, investigate their physical and chemical properties safely, and use evidence to explain why elements suit their uses. Each lesson cycles through predict, observe, explain, Driving Question Board and model building, so the family-trends model grows throughout the unit.
UNIT.phenomenon: In a Kenyan kitchen and compound, many everyday objects are made of different elements. The sufuria for cooking ugali is aluminium, the electric cable of the jiko or kettle is copper, the mabati roof is iron coated with zinc, drinking water in Mombasa is treated with chlorine, and street lamps along Thika Road glow with sodium light. Yet sodium metal itself reacts violently with water and must be stored under oil, while chlorine is a poisonous gas that makes water safe to drink. Students observe a collection of these objects and a demonstration of a small piece of sodium in water, and wonder why elements with such different, even dangerous, properties each end up as a safe and useful item, and why a given element is chosen for a given job and not another.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Table salt (sodium chloride) on our ugali and nyama choma is safe to eat, though it is made from a violently reactive metal and a poisonous gas.
• Magnesium ribbon burns with a bright white flame, which is why it is used in flares and fireworks.
• Neon and other noble gas signs and lamps glow brightly with colour, yet the noble gases hardly react with anything.
• Iron nails rust while zinc-coated mabati roofs last for years, and copper wires conduct current for decades.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why does each element behave and get used the way it does, and how can the periodic table help us predict which element is right for which job in Kenyan daily life?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Anchoring phenomenon. Students examine Kenyan objects (aluminium sufuria, copper wire, mabati, salt) and watch a sodium demonstration. They predict why different elements are used for different jobs and build the Driving Question Board with initial questions.
Lesson 2: Chemical families. Students research and sort the first twenty elements into alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens and noble gases, and note where the transition metals sit. They draft an initial family model.
Lesson 3: Physical properties of the families. Students investigate appearance, hardness, density, melting and conductivity of samples and secondary data across families, and record patterns in a table.
Lesson 4: Alkali metals. Using teacher demonstrations of sodium (and lithium or potassium if available) with air and water, students observe reactivity, write balanced equations, link reactivity to the single outer electron, and apply safety and first aid rules.
Lesson 5: Alkaline earth metals. Students investigate magnesium with air, water and dilute acid, write balanced equations, and compare its reactivity with sodium to revise the model.
Lesson 6: Halogens and noble gases. Students study chlorine's reactions (via demonstration, video and simulation) and its use in water treatment in Mombasa and Nairobi, then explain why noble gases are unreactive and suited to road lighting and signs.
Lesson 7: Transition metals. Students research and discuss copper, iron, zinc and lead and their uses (wiring, mabati, galvanising, batteries), and match properties to uses with digital and print sources.
Lesson 8: Putting it together. Students complete the family model, answer the Driving Question Board, and explain, using evidence, why an element is chosen for a given use, for example by recommending an element for a new Kenyan product. They reflect on safety and care for self and others.

LESSONS.title: The Sufuria, Wire, Mabati, Salt, Chlorine and Sodium-Lamp Puzzle
LESSONS.aresKeywords: element, compound, chemical family, group, period, properties, reactivity, sodium, chlorine, aluminium, copper, zinc, periodic table, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the unit by confronting learners with the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle: everyday Kenyan objects made from elements with very different, sometimes dangerous, properties. Learners predict, observe and question why each element suits its job.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) name the elements in six Kenyan anchor objects (aluminium sufuria, copper wire, mabati of iron coated with zinc, table salt NaCl, Mombasa water treated with chlorine, Thika Road sodium lamp); (b) state that these elements have very different properties and that sodium reacts violently with water while the same element is combined in safe salt; (c) pose questions about why an element suits a particular job.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (initial ideas); asking questions and defining problems (NGSS SEP 1); planning predictions; observing and recording; constructing explanations from evidence; communicating and collaborating in groups.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how everyday materials work; respect for others' opinions when sharing predictions (Value: Respect); care for self and others by observing safety near reactive elements (Value: Love). PCI: Safety and security, and Road safety (street lighting). Appreciation of the uses of elements of the periodic table in day-to-day life.
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the anchoring lesson. It sets up the Driving Question: Why does each element behave and get used the way it does, and how can the periodic table help us predict which element is right for which job in Kenyan daily life? Learners start the Driving Question Board (DQB) with the categories Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety, and start the class family model (a wall periodic table). Lessons 2 to 8 return to these questions, beginning with Lesson 2 on chemical families and the periodic table layout. No later content (families, outer electron explanations, equations) is taught here.
slo.safetyNotes: Sodium demonstration is by the teacher ONLY (Mr. Otieno model): safety screen, goggles and lab coat, pea-sized piece (about 0.1 g) cut under paraffin oil, dropped into a trough of water; learners stand at least 2 m back behind the screen and wear goggles. Learners never touch or handle sodium. Keep sodium stored under paraffin oil, with no water near the store. Dispose of residues as directed by the teacher and have a first aid kit on hand. Learners handle only the safe objects (sufuria, wire, mabati, salt) with clean hands; no tasting of lab materials. Do not bring chlorine gas to class; use only the water-treatment information or a picture or video.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru, a food seller in Mombasa, cooks ugali in an aluminium sufuria and asks why her pot is safe while chlorine in her tap water is poisonous as a gas. In this lesson learners examine a collection of Kenyan objects (aluminium sufuria, copper wire from a kettle or jiko cable, mabati of iron coated with zinc, table salt) and look at information on Mombasa water treated with chlorine (about 0.5 mg/L) and Thika Road sodium lamps glowing yellow-orange. They first predict what the sodium in the lamp and salt would do in water, then watch the teacher demonstrate a pea-sized piece of sodium in water: it floats, fizzes, darts about, melts into a ball, and the solution turns pink with phenolphthalein, showing an alkali (NaOH) forms. They are puzzled that this dangerous element is also part of safe salt. In groups they try to explain the puzzle and record questions on sticky notes for the DQB, sorted into Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety. They finish by drawing an initial model of why an element suits a job. Learners do not yet explain the puzzle fully; the unit does that.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners pass round the anchor objects: an aluminium sufuria (from a Gikomba jua kali artisan), copper wire from a kettle or jiko cable, a piece of galvanised mabati, and a bowl of table salt (NaCl). The teacher reads out Mama Wanjiru's question and gives facts: Mombasa water works adds chlorine at about 0.5 mg/L, and Thika Road lamps glow yellow-orange with sodium vapour. Learners write individual predictions in their notebooks: (1) 'What do you think would happen if a small piece of sodium, the element in salt and in the street lamp, were dropped into water?' (2) 'Why do you think each object is made from the element it is made from and not another?' They then share in the group and draw a quick prediction sketch.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the objects on a table before the lesson and say: 'Look at these ordinary things from a Kenyan kitchen and compound. Each one is made from a different element. What do you notice?' Hand out the objects and allow 3 minutes. Read Mama Wanjiru's question aloud. Ask: 'Sodium is in this salt, and it is in the Thika Road lamp. Write down what you think a pea-sized piece of pure sodium will do in water.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after the question before anyone speaks. Then cold-call 4 learners from different groups (e.g. Akinyi's group and Kiprop's group) to share predictions without evaluating them: 'Thank you. Tell me what makes you think that.' Record 3-4 predictions on the board under 'Our first ideas'. Say: 'We will not say who is right yet; we will test our ideas.' Circulate and note learners who link properties to jobs, such as the sufuria being light or the wire conducting electricity.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-before-observe with Think-Pair-Share: writing a prediction individually first exposes prior ideas, and sharing in groups lets learners compare them. The prediction is later compared with observations, which creates a need to know and supports the NGSS practice of asking questions and defining problems.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each learner writes a prediction with a reason (look for at least one reason per notebook). Check that predictions mention an observable outcome (floats, fizzes, nothing happens, explodes). Listen for misconceptions, such as 'salt is dangerous because it has sodium' or 'all metals sink and are safe', and note them for the DQB. Tally on a checklist how many learners can name the metal in at least 3 of the objects.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners stand behind the safety screen, wearing goggles, at least 2 m back, while the teacher (Mr. Otieno model) takes sodium from its paraffin oil, cuts a pea-sized piece (about 0.1 g) and shows the shiny cut face before it dulls. The piece is dropped into a trough of water. Learners record what they see in a table: appearance of sodium (soft, silvery, cut with a knife, stored under oil), behaviour in water (floats, fizzes, darts about, melts into a ball), and the colour change when phenolphthalein is added (turns pink, so NaOH, an alkali, has formed). They then examine the anchor data: the sufuria, wire, mabati and salt, a picture of the Mombasa water works and of the Thika Road lamps. They compare the properties of sodium with salt and with the other objects in a 'What I saw / What I know' table.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the demonstration, say: 'This is a teacher demonstration only. Nobody touches sodium. Goggles on, stay behind the line.' Check that every learner has goggles. Explain why sodium is kept under paraffin oil: 'No water near the store.' Ask: 'What will you look for? Write down three things to observe.' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Do the demonstration slowly and narrate only what is seen, not why: 'The piece is floating. I can hear fizzing.' Pause after dropping it for learners to watch. Add 2 drops of phenolphthalein and ask: 'What colour is it now?' Cold-call 3 learners to describe what they saw using only observations (not explanations). Then say: 'The same element, sodium, is in the salt in Mama Wanjiru's ugali and in the Thika Road lamps. Compare what you saw with the salt in your hand.' Ask: 'What is surprising?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Cold-call 2 more learners. Show the chlorine information: 'Chlorine is a poisonous gas, but Mombasa water works adds about 0.5 mg per litre to make our water safe.' Dispose of residues as directed and keep the screen in place until finished.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collecting evidence through a teacher demonstration with a structured observation table (separating observation from inference). This builds the habit of using evidence, and the 'surprise' between a violent element and safe salt generates authentic questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the observation tables for at least 3 accurate observations of sodium (floats, fizzes, darts about, melts into a ball, pink with phenolphthalein) and that observations are separated from explanations. Note who follows the safety rules (goggles on, 2 m back). Listen for learners expressing surprise or noticing the contrast between sodium and salt or chlorine and safe drinking water.

framework.learnerExperience: In their groups, learners use a 'puzzle map' on a manila sheet to put the six anchor objects (sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, Mombasa water, Thika Road lamp) in a ring around the question 'Why does each element suit its job?'. For each object they write the element (Al, Cu, Fe and Zn, NaCl, Cl, Na), one property they know or think matters (for example light, conducts electricity, does not rust, kills germs, glows yellow) and one thing they wonder. They then try to explain in 2-3 sentences how sodium can be dangerous alone and yet safe as salt, and why chlorine can be poisonous as a gas but safe in water. They compare their first predictions with what they saw and mark them 'supported', 'not supported' or 'not sure'. Groups share their best attempts in a gallery walk and mark ideas they agree or disagree with using different-coloured sticky dots.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your task is to use the evidence you saw to make a first explanation of the puzzle. It is fine to say we are not sure.' Give 10 minutes for group work and circulate with prompts such as: 'What evidence from the demonstration supports that?' and 'Is the property you chose useful for that job? Why?' Do not give the answer (outer electrons and families are for later lessons). If asked 'Why does sodium react so much?' say: 'Great question. Put it on a sticky note for the Driving Question Board; we will investigate it.' Run a gallery walk for 5 minutes. Then ask: 'Which ideas did several groups share? Which ideas are different?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups to share one idea and one wondering. Record common ideas and disagreements on the board. Highlight that different elements have very different properties and that each is useful in a different job, which is the pattern to explain. Praise ideas that use evidence.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Group puzzle mapping followed by a gallery walk and a claim-evidence-reasoning check: connecting each object to an element, a property and a question helps learners notice patterns across objects. Honest initial explanations, with agree and disagree dots, make gaps in understanding visible and motivate the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that puzzle maps correctly name the element in at least 5 of 6 objects (Al, Cu, Fe and Zn, NaCl, Cl, Na) and link at least 3 to a property. Look for explanations that use evidence from the demonstration instead of just opinion. Note the misconceptions to revisit (for example 'salt is just sodium', 'chlorine in water is a gas bubble', or 'dangerous elements are never useful'). Use a thumbs up/side/down check on 'I can explain why sodium in salt is safe' to gauge confidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Akinyi and Kiprop (DQB keepers for the class) help to set up a wall chart with four columns: Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety. Each learner writes at least 2 questions on sticky notes (for example Akinyi: 'Why is sodium so dangerous?', Kiprop: 'Why do street lamps glow yellow?', 'Why is the sufuria made of aluminium and not iron?', 'How can poisonous chlorine make water safe?'). Learners place their notes in the best column and read others' notes. As a class they group similar questions and agree a final Driving Question: 'Why does each element behave and get used the way it does, and how can the periodic table help us predict which element is right for which job in Kenyan daily life?' They then choose three questions they most want answered.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Good scientists write down what they wonder. Write at least two questions about the puzzle on sticky notes: one question per note, starting with Why or How.' Give 5 minutes. Model one example: 'Why is the mabati coated with zinc?' Circulate and help rephrase yes/no questions into 'why' or 'how' questions. Invite Akinyi and Kiprop to post the first notes and sort the rest into the four columns. Ask: 'Which questions are alike? Which column is missing questions?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to read a question aloud and say which column it belongs to. Read out the Driving Question and ask the class to say it in their own words. Explain that the board will be revisited at the end of every lesson, with answers added as evidence is found. Photograph the DQB. Say: 'Today we will not answer them. In the next lesson we look at how the elements are arranged.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with categorised student questions: using learners' own questions gives ownership and a visible record of what the class needs to figure out, and sorting them into categories shows the shape of the unit. It supports asking questions and defining problems.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count questions: each learner has at least 2 on sticky notes. Check that at least half are 'why' or 'how' questions and are placed in sensible columns. Notice whether questions go beyond naming objects, for example linking properties to uses or asking why sodium is reactive. Note learners who have not contributed and invite them with a cold-call or a buddy.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner draws an initial model in their notebook titled 'Why does an element suit its job?'. The model includes: the six anchor objects, the element in each, arrows linking each element to one property and one job, and a box showing sodium and chlorine together becoming salt with a question mark ('what changes?'). They add labels such as 'dangerous alone / safe in salt' and 'unsure' where they cannot explain. They then add to the class family model, a large wall periodic table, by placing sticky labels on Na, Cl, Al, Cu, Fe and Zn with the job each does (for example Na: street lamp and salt; Al: sufuria). They write a one-line 'What I think now' statement and a 'What I still need to find out' statement.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw your first model. It will be wrong in places, and that is the point. We will revise it in every lesson.' Display an example of a model with arrows from objects to properties. Give 8 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'What does this arrow mean?' and 'What do you want to find out here?' Invite learners to place labels on the class wall periodic table and ask: 'Where do you think each of these elements sits? Does position matter?' (Do not teach families yet.) WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one part of their models. Finish with an exit ticket: 'Write one thing you saw today that surprised you and one question you will check in the next lesson.' Collect models and keep them for revision in later lessons. Link ahead: 'In Lesson 2 we will see how elements are grouped into chemical families in the periodic table.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model drawing and a class family model on the wall periodic table: representing ideas visually and revising them over the unit lets learners see their own progress. Marking 'unsure' parts turns gaps into investigation goals and supports developing and using models.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that models include at least 4 anchor objects with the correct element, at least 3 links from element to property or job, and a visible attempt to show sodium and chlorine in salt. Look for 'unsure' labels as evidence of honest thinking. Use exit tickets to see if learners can state one surprise and one question. Review models after class to plan how to address common ideas in Lessons 2 and 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did every learner see the sodium demonstration clearly and safely from behind the screen? Which predictions were most common, and which misconceptions (for example that salt is the same as sodium) appeared? Did learners ask questions beyond naming objects, such as why sodium is reactive or why chlorine is used in tiny doses? Which DQB columns (Properties, Reactivity, Uses, Safety) had the fewest questions, and how can I encourage more? Were all learners, including quieter ones, heard through cold-calls and wait time? Check that the sodium, paraffin oil and goggles were handled and stored correctly. Plan to open Lesson 2 by returning to the DQB and the wall periodic table.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that everyday Kenyan objects are made from different elements: aluminium sufuria, copper wire, iron mabati coated with zinc, salt (NaCl), chlorine-treated Mombasa water and sodium-lamp light on Thika Road. We also saw sodium float, fizz, dart about and melt in water, and turn the solution pink with phenolphthalein.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that elements have very different properties, and some, like sodium, are dangerous on their own, yet each is useful and chosen for a job. We now have many questions about why an element suits a job, recorded on the DQB under Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Our first explanation is that each element is used for the job that its properties suit, but we cannot yet explain why sodium is violent alone yet safe in salt, or why chlorine is poisonous as a gas yet safe in tiny amounts in water. We will use the periodic table and later investigations to answer these questions.

LESSONS.title: Chemical Families: Sorting the First Twenty Elements by Position in the Periodic Table
LESSONS.aresKeywords: chemical family, group, period, alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases, transition metals, outer electrons, periodic table

slo.purpose: To help learners see that elements are sorted into chemical families by their position in the periodic table, and that group number links to similar behaviour. This lets them place the elements behind the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle on a family map and begin predicting which element suits which job.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) identify chemical families in the periodic table; (b) classify elements of the periodic table into their chemical families. Learners will know that: alkali metals are Group 1 (Li, Na, K), alkaline earth metals are Group 2 (Be, Mg, Ca), halogens are Group 17 (F, Cl), noble gases are Group 18 (He, Ne, Ar), and transition metals sit in the central block from Period 4 (Sc to Zn, including Fe, Cu, Zn). H, B, C, N, O, Al, Si, P and S are not in any of the four families. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons (Group 1 = 1, Group 2 = 2, Group 17 = 7, Group 18 = 8, with He = 2) and so behave similarly.
slo.skills: NGSS Science and Engineering Practices: Analysing and Interpreting Data (sorting and finding patterns in the first twenty elements table); Developing and Using Models (drafting the initial class family model on the wall periodic table); Constructing Explanations (using position and outer electrons to justify family membership). KICD core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (sorting and arranging the first twenty elements according to their similarities); Digital literacy (using available digital and print media to research element categories).
slo.attitudes: Values: Respect (recognising every group member's input when sorting and debating placements); Unity (taking turns in roles during the card sort). PCI: Life skills (problem solving) as the learner arranges the first twenty elements into groups and periods. Learners appreciate that a position on the periodic table helps predict an element's behaviour in daily Kenyan life.
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 produced the puzzle (sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, Mombasa chlorinated water, Thika Road sodium lamp, and the sodium-in-water demonstration) and DQB questions about why an element suits a job. Lesson 2 gives learners the first organising tool: the family map of the periodic table. They locate the anchor elements (Al, Cu, Fe, Zn, Na, Cl) on it and draft an initial family model. Lesson 3 will use these families to organise physical property data, and Lessons 4 to 7 will explain family behaviour in detail. This lesson does not explain why families react as they do. It only establishes that position and group number link to similar behaviour.
slo.safetyNotes: This is a paper and wall-chart lesson, so no hazardous chemicals are handled. If the teacher shows sealed samples (Mg ribbon, Al foil, Cu wire, Fe nail, Zn strip), learners wear goggles and handle only those. Sodium, potassium and lithium are NOT handled by learners and are not brought out in this lesson. Remind learners of the Lesson 1 rule: never touch sodium with bare hands, and keep water away from stored sodium (kept under paraffin oil). Keep the aisles clear while learners move to the wall periodic table.

LESSONS.overview: Mr. Otieno's Grade 10 class in Kisumu returns to the DQB from Lesson 1, where Akinyi asked why sodium is dangerous and Kiprop asked why street lamps glow yellow. Learners first predict how the elements behind the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle might be grouped. They then research and sort the first twenty elements (symbols, atomic numbers Z and positions) into alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens and noble gases, and note where the transition metals sit. Next they explain why elements in the same group might behave alike, using outer electron counts (Group 1 = 1, Group 2 = 2, Group 17 = 7, Group 18 = 8). They add new questions to the DQB and annotate the large wall periodic table with the anchor elements, producing a first draft of the class family model. Mama Wanjiru's question (why her aluminium sufuria is safe while chlorine gas is poisonous) is treated as a family question: which families do Al and Cl belong to?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Lesson 1 anchor list (aluminium sufuria, copper wire, mabati of iron coated with zinc, table salt, Mombasa chlorinated water, Thika Road sodium lamp). On a half-sheet, individually, they write the symbol and Z of each element: Al 13, Cu 29, Fe 26, Zn 30, Na 11, Cl 17. They then answer: 'If a class of elements had to be sorted into families, which of these six would you put together, and what would you base it on?' They draw their prediction as a quick sketch: a rough blank periodic table with the six elements placed where they think they belong. They share with a partner for 2 minutes. Learners are told that their sketch is a prediction and that it is fine to be wrong.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Lesson 1 anchor objects and the DQB. Say: 'Yesterday we wondered why sodium is dangerous but salt is safe, and why a sufuria and a wire are made of different elements. Today we ask: do elements come in families, like people in a Luo or Kalenjin clan, with shared traits?' Give the six symbols and Z values on the board. Say: 'Silently, for 3 minutes, predict which of these elements might belong together and why.' WAIT TIME: after asking 'What did you base your grouping on?', wait 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners (including Akinyi and Kiprop) using the name cards, and ask each only 'What did you base it on?' Do not correct predictions. Record the bases offered (colour, use, hardness, state, position) on the board under 'Our Ideas for Grouping'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with individual prediction first. Committing to a written, drawn prediction makes learners' existing ideas visible, so they can later compare them with evidence and notice what they had to revise. Recording the bases for grouping on the board gives the class a shared starting point.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the sketches while circulating. Look for: (1) learners who group by use or appearance only (for example, 'sufuria and wire are both kitchen items'); (2) learners who mention position or number; (3) learners who place Na and Cl together because they make salt. Tally on a clipboard how many sketches group by use, appearance or position. Success indicator: at least 4 learners can name a basis for grouping, even if it is incorrect, and every learner has placed all six elements on the sketch.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners research and sort the first twenty elements. Each group gets (a) a blank periodic table outline for Periods 1 to 4, (b) 20 element cards (H1, He2, Li3, Be4, B5, C6, N7, O8, F9, Ne10, Na11, Mg12, Al13, Si14, P15, S16, Cl17, Ar18, K19, Ca20) showing symbol, Z and electron arrangement where known (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Cl 2,8,7; Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8), and (c) a textbook or tablet with a periodic table. Step 1: place the cards in order of Z in the correct rows and columns (groups = vertical columns, periods = horizontal rows). Step 2: use print or digital resources to find the family names for Groups 1, 2, 17 and 18 and mark them with colour pencils (alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases). Step 3: sort each of the 20 cards into one of five piles: alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases, or 'not in these four families' (H, B, C, N, O, Al, Si, P, S). Step 4: locate the transition metals block between Group 2 and Group 13 beginning at Period 4 (Sc to Zn) and place cards for Fe26, Cu29 and Zn30 in it. Roles: reader, card handler, recorder, reporter, rotated midway. Learners complete a Family Sorting Table with columns: family, group number, elements from the first twenty, number of outer electrons.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials and review the roles: 'Everyone takes a turn. The reader reads aloud, the card handler places cards, the recorder writes, the reporter speaks.' Model the first placement on the board: 'Na is Z = 11, so it comes after Ne at the start of Period 3. Which group is it in?' Circulate to each group at least once. Ask: 'What do you notice about the elements in the same column?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after the question before rephrasing. Probe: 'Where did you put H, and why is it not in a family with Li and Na?' Confirm that H is a non-metal that is not placed in any of the four families. Say: 'Aluminium is Z = 13, in Period 3, and it is a metal, but it is not in any of our four families. Mark it as other.' Stop groups at the 25-minute mark. Cold-call 5 groups to read out one family each from their Family Sorting Table: 'Group 3, read us the alkali metals.' Ask the class to show thumbs up or down to check. Then ask a group to show where the transition metals sit. Clarify that Pb (Z = 82) is beyond the first twenty and is not sorted today. Remind learners that the anchor object elements will be located on the table in the next phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data sorting and pattern-seeking (structured card sort). Learners physically sort real data into categories, so patterns (family names matching columns, outer electrons matching group numbers) become visible from the data and are not just told. Rotating roles ensures all learners engage in the analysis.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect the Family Sorting Table from each group and check against the key. Indicators: alkali metals Li, Na, K placed in Group 1; alkaline earth metals Be, Mg, Ca in Group 2; halogens F, Cl in Group 17; noble gases He, Ne, Ar in Group 18; H, B, C, N, O, Al, Si, P and S marked as not in the four families; transition metals placed in the central block from Period 4. Success indicator: at least 80% of groups sort 16 or more of the 20 elements correctly, and every group correctly states that transition metals start at Period 4. Note groups that misplace Al or H, and reteach at their table.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in the same groups, then share with the whole class. Part A (10 minutes): They use their Family Sorting Table to answer: (1) What do the elements Li, Na and K have in common in their electron arrangements (2,1; 2,8,1; 2,8,8,1)? (2) What is the number of outer electrons in Mg and Ca (Group 2)? Cl (Group 17)? Ne and Ar (Group 18)? (3) What pattern links group number to outer electrons (Group 1 = 1, Group 2 = 2, Group 17 = 7, Group 18 = 8, He = 2 as a full first shell)? Part B (10 minutes): Each group writes a claim-evidence-reasoning statement: 'Claim: Elements in the same group are likely to behave similarly. Evidence: ... Reasoning: ...' Part C (8 minutes): Using the anchor data, they locate the six elements of the puzzle on their table and name their family or block: Na is an alkali metal (Group 1); Cl is a halogen (Group 17); Al is a metal not in the four families (Group 13); Fe, Cu and Zn are transition metals. They answer Mama Wanjiru's question in one sentence: 'Her sufuria is aluminium and chlorine is a halogen, so they belong to different parts of the periodic table.' Learners note that they cannot yet say why those positions give those behaviours; that is for later lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Look at your Family Sorting Table. What is the same for every element in one column?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds, then allow pair talk for 1 minute. Cold-call 3 pairs and write their ideas on the board: same number of outer electrons, same group number, similar position. Then say: 'Group 1 elements each have one outer electron. Group 2 has two, Group 17 has seven, Group 18 has eight, except helium, which has two because its first shell is full.' Ask: 'What might the number of outer electrons have to do with how an element behaves?' WAIT TIME: wait 15 seconds. Accept ideas as hypotheses and say: 'We will test this idea in the next lessons. Today we only note the link between group number and outer electrons.' Do not explain reactivity or why Na is dangerous; say: 'Hold onto Akinyi's question about sodium. Lesson 4 will answer it.' Give the CER frame on the board. Check 3 claim statements by cold-calling and asking each speaker: 'What is your evidence from the table?' For Part C, ask: 'Where does copper sit? Which block?' and 'Is aluminium in one of our four families? How do you know?' Praise careful use of the words 'group', 'period' and 'chemical family' and correct 'row' and 'column' confusion: group is vertical, period is horizontal.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with discourse. Writing a claim, tying it to table evidence and giving reasoning forces learners to connect position, group number and outer electrons, rather than memorise family names. Pair talk before cold-calling lets every learner rehearse an answer first.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read the written CER statements. Indicators: a correct claim that same-group elements behave similarly; evidence citing at least two specific elements and their outer electron counts (for example Li 2,1 and Na 2,8,1 each have 1 outer electron); reasoning that links group number to similar behaviour. Check that Na, Cl, Al, Fe, Cu and Zn are all located correctly. Success indicator: at least 75% of learners write a CER statement with a correct claim and at least one correct piece of evidence. Misconception to watch: learners who say all metals are in one family, or who say hydrogen belongs to Group 1 as an alkali metal.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB, divided into the four columns Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety. Each learner writes one new question on a sticky note based on today's findings, for example: 'Why do elements in the same family behave alike?' (Reactivity), 'Are all alkali metals as dangerous as sodium?' (Safety), 'Why is aluminium not in a family like sodium?' (Properties), 'Is chlorine like other halogens?' (Reactivity), 'Why are the noble gases used in signs?' (Uses), 'Why is copper in a block with iron?' (Properties). They place the notes in a column and cluster similar questions. Akinyi and Kiprop, the DQB keepers, review old Lesson 1 questions. Learners put a tick on any Lesson 1 question that today's family map partly helps with (for example Kiprop's question on the yellow lamp now has a clue: sodium is an alkali metal). They do not mark any question as answered yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take 2 minutes to write one new question you have now that you did not have before.' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after the instruction before anyone moves. Cold-call 4 learners to read their question aloud and say which column it belongs in: 'Which column does your question go in, and why?' Ask Akinyi and Kiprop to cluster similar notes and read one cluster title. Ask: 'Which old questions from Lesson 1 can we now say something about?' Cold-call 2 learners. Point out that most answers are still missing and that the DQB will guide the next lessons: physical properties (Lesson 3), alkali metals (Lesson 4), and so on. Do not answer any questions today. Say: 'Good questions are more valuable than quick answers.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question clustering. Learners generate and sort questions from new evidence, so they see how today's learning leads to new puzzles and owns the direction of the unit. Linking old questions to the new family map shows progress without prematurely answering.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect the sticky notes and check quality. Indicators: each question is specific to families or to the anchor elements (not 'what are elements?'), is placed in a sensible column, and shows a link between position and behaviour or use. Success indicator: at least 80% of learners produce a question that mentions a family, group, or one of the anchor elements. Tally how many questions fall in each column and note which families learners are most curious about, to guide Lessons 3 and 4.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners build the first draft of the class family model on the large wall periodic table. In turns, each group sticks coloured labels on the wall chart for the first twenty elements and the transition block: orange for alkali metals, blue for alkaline earth metals, green for halogens, purple for noble gases, grey for transition metals. They then annotate the six anchor elements with small picture cards: Al (sufuria), Cu (wire), Fe and Zn (mabati), Na (salt and Thika Road lamp), Cl (Mombasa water), and write the family or block name under each. Beside the chart, each learner copies a personal model into their notebook with a key. Below it they complete a short statement: 'In my family model, elements in the same group have the same number of ______ outer electrons, so I predict they will ______.' They add a 'What we still don't know' box listing at least two open questions (for example why sodium reacts violently with water, why noble gases are used in lamps, which properties make Al suit the sufuria).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'This wall table is our family model. It is a first draft, and we will revise it every lesson.' Hand each group two element labels at a time so all groups get a turn, with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before each group places its labels so peers can check. Cold-call 3 learners to challenge a placement: 'Is Al correctly placed? How do you know?' Remind: 'Aluminium and hydrogen are not in the four families. Mark them differently.' As Akinyi and Kiprop keep the model, ask them to read the labels aloud. Prompt: 'Use the model to predict: will potassium behave more like sodium or like chlorine? Say why in one sentence.' Cold-call 3 learners. Accept predictions as ideas to test, for example 'like sodium, same group, one outer electron'. Do not confirm reactivity details. Explain homework: find one more object at home or in the market (for example a jua kali item from Gikomba, a battery, or a nail) and name one element in it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building. Learners draft a visible model that links position, family and outer electrons to the anchor objects, and then use it to make a prediction. Because the model is annotated each lesson, they can see it grow and can identify gaps (the 'don't know' box) that drive later investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the notebook models and the wall chart. Indicators: all 20 elements and the transition block placed in the correct colour-coded family; the six anchor elements correctly located; H and Al marked as not in the four families; a prediction that uses group number (for example K will behave like Na). Success indicator: at least 80% of learners have a correct model and one reasoned prediction, and each lists at least two open questions. Use the 'What we still don't know' boxes to plan Lesson 3 on comparing physical properties.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners sort the first twenty elements using position and group number rather than guessing from the names? Which groups misplaced H or Al, and why? (2) Could learners state the link between group number and outer electrons without being led, or did they need prompting? (3) Did I resist explaining why Na is dangerous and keep that for Lesson 4? (4) Did the cold-calling and 10-15 second WAIT TIME give quieter learners, including those who sat at the back, a chance to speak? (5) Were the new DQB questions linked to families and the anchor objects? (6) What misconceptions emerged (for example that all metals form one family, or that hydrogen is an alkali metal)? Plan to address them in Lesson 3 with the physical property data. Note learners who need extra support with reading the periodic table and arrange pairing with a confident partner.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We sorted the first twenty elements by position on the periodic table. Li, Na and K are in Group 1 (alkali metals); Be, Mg and Ca are in Group 2 (alkaline earth metals); F and Cl are in Group 17 (halogens); He, Ne and Ar are in Group 18 (noble gases). H, B, C, N, O, Al, Si, P and S are not in any of these four families. The transition metals, including Fe, Cu and Zn, sit in the central block starting from Period 4.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Elements are grouped into chemical families by their position in the periodic table. Groups are vertical columns and periods are horizontal rows. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons (Group 1 = 1, Group 2 = 2, Group 17 = 7, Group 18 = 8, with He = 2), which links group number to similar behaviour.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Sodium (Na, Thika Road lamp and salt) is an alkali metal, chlorine (Cl, Mombasa water) is a halogen, aluminium (sufuria) is a metal not in the four families, and copper (wire), iron and zinc (mabati) are transition metals. So the elements in our puzzle come from different parts of the periodic table, and a family's position can help us predict behaviour. We still need evidence on their properties and reactivity to explain why each element suits its job.

LESSONS.title: Physical Properties of the Families: Finding Patterns in Density, Melting Point, Hardness and Conductivity
LESSONS.aresKeywords: physical properties, density, melting point, hardness, conductivity, chemical family, pattern, alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, transition metals, halogens, noble gases, group, period

slo.purpose: Learners compare the physical properties of elements from different chemical families, using samples and a secondary data table, to find patterns across and within families. This gives them evidence for why an element suits a job in the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) compare hardness, density, melting point and conductivity for selected elements from the alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, transition metals, halogens and noble gases; (b) identify patterns, e.g. Na, K and Li are soft, low-density, low-melting metals that float on water (1.00 g/cm3), while Mg, Ca and the transition metals are denser and melt at higher temperatures; (c) state that metals in the data table conduct electricity while Cl2, Ne and Ar do not; (d) connect a property to a job, e.g. copper's excellent conductivity for wire and aluminium's low density for the sufuria.
slo.skills: Science and Engineering Practices: (1) Planning and carrying out investigations: testing hardness, density and conductivity of Mg, Al, Cu, Fe and Zn samples with goggles on. (2) Analysing and interpreting data: organising the secondary data table by family and finding patterns. (3) Using mathematics: calculating density as mass divided by volume and comparing values with water at 1.00 g/cm3. (4) Constructing explanations from evidence. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that evidence from careful measurement lets us predict which element is right for which job. Values: Respect (listening to group members' interpretations of the data) and Unity (taking assigned roles in the group practical). Learners also show care and responsibility for themselves and others when handling samples.
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 organised the first 20 elements into chemical families by position in the periodic table. This lesson uses those family groupings to organise physical data and search for patterns. It prepares Lesson 4 (why alkali metals are soft, light and very reactive), Lesson 5 (Mg is denser and higher melting than Na) and Lesson 7 (transition metals as strong, dense, high-melting conductors). Learners start to see why sodium is stored under oil and cut with a knife, why aluminium suits a sufuria and why copper suits wire. Reasons based on outer electrons are left for Lessons 4 to 6.
slo.safetyNotes: Goggles on for all practical work. Learners handle only Mg ribbon and Al, Cu, Fe and Zn samples. Na, K and Li are never handled by learners. Mr. Otieno shows them only as sealed, labelled samples under paraffin oil, or uses a photo or video. No water near stored sodium. Chlorine is treated as secondary data only; no chlorine gas is prepared. Use low-voltage dry cells for the conductivity circuit and keep it away from water. Handle the cut edges of metal strips carefully. Dispose of samples as the teacher directs, and keep the first aid kit on the bench.

LESSONS.overview: Mr. Otieno opens with Mama Wanjiru's question from the Mombasa market: why is her aluminium sufuria safe on the fire while the sodium in the demo was dangerous? Learners first predict how the families differ in density, melting point, hardness and conductivity. In the Observe phase, groups test real samples of Mg, Al, Cu, Fe and Zn for appearance, hardness (scratch test), density (mass and water displacement) and conductivity (simple circuit). They then study a secondary data table covering Na, K, Li, Mg, Ca, Fe, Cu, Zn, Al, Pb, Cl2, Ne and Ar. In the Explain phase, learners sort the data by family and identify patterns within and across families. Akinyi and Kiprop add new questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) under 'Properties', and learners annotate the class family model with property labels. Learners finish with an initial model linking family position to physical properties and to jobs such as sufuria, wire and mabati.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the anchor objects (aluminium sufuria, copper wire, mabati roof of iron coated with zinc) and the sodium demo from Lesson 1. Working individually for 3 minutes, then in pairs, they complete a prediction table with four rows: density, melting point, hardness and conductivity. For each row they predict whether sodium (Group 1), magnesium (Group 2), copper (transition), aluminium and chlorine would be high or low, and write one sentence of reasoning, e.g. 'Sodium was cut under oil with a knife, so I predict it is soft.' They also answer: 'Sodium floated in the trough. What does floating tell us about its density compared with water at 1.00 g/cm3?'
framework.teacherMoves: Mr. Otieno holds up the sufuria, a piece of copper wire and a strip of mabati and says: 'Mama Wanjiru cooks ugali in this aluminium sufuria every day. Last lesson we grouped elements into families. Today I want your best guess: do elements in the same family look and behave alike when we compare them physically?' He gives 3 minutes of silent individual writing, then 2 minutes for pairs. He then says: 'Think about the sodium we saw floating. What does floating tell you?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. He cold-calls 4 learners, using no hands up, to share one prediction and reasoning, and records each prediction on the board without correcting it. He asks: 'Who disagrees with that, and why?' Pairs must give a reason, not only an answer. Predictions are photographed or copied for return in the Explain phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas through a prediction table. Putting ideas in writing before any evidence is shown commits learners to a testable claim, so they can later compare evidence with their own thinking. Learners link everyday observations to scientific ideas such as density and floating, which strengthens connections to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) at least 80% of learners have a complete prediction table with reasoning, not just answers; (2) learners link floating sodium to density lower than 1.00 g/cm3; (3) Mr. Otieno notes common ideas such as 'all metals are hard and heavy' or 'all metals have the same melting point' for later testing; (4) Mr. Otieno tallies how many predict sodium is softer than copper. Learners who write only one-word answers get a prompt: 'What did you see in the demo that makes you say that?'

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (about 25 minutes): Hands-on testing. Groups of four, with goggles on, take roles: materials manager, tester, recorder and reporter. They test Mg ribbon and Al, Cu, Fe and Zn samples. (1) Appearance: colour and shine. (2) Hardness: scratch each sample with a nail or the edge of a coin and rank them from softest to hardest. (3) Density: measure mass on a balance, find volume by water displacement in a measuring cylinder, calculate mass divided by volume in g/cm3 and compare with water at 1.00 g/cm3; they predict, then check, whether each sample sinks. (4) Conductivity: connect each sample in a circuit with a dry cell and bulb or buzzer and record whether it lights. They record results in a table. Part B (about 15 minutes): Secondary data. Learners receive the physical data table: Na: 0.97 g/cm3, 98 C, soft, conducts. K: 0.86 g/cm3, 63 C, soft, conducts. Li: 0.53 g/cm3, 181 C, soft, conducts. Mg: 1.74 g/cm3, 650 C, harder, conducts. Ca: 1.55 g/cm3, 842 C, harder, conducts. Fe: 7.87 g/cm3, 1538 C, hard, conducts. Cu: 8.96 g/cm3, 1085 C, hard, excellent conductor. Zn: 7.14 g/cm3, 420 C, conducts. Al: 2.70 g/cm3, 660 C, conducts. Pb: 11.34 g/cm3, 327 C, soft and heavy, poor-to-moderate conductor. Cl2: greenish-yellow gas, melts -101 C, boils -34 C, non-conductor. Ne: colourless gas, boils -246 C, non-conductor. Ar: colourless gas, boils -186 C, non-conductor. Mr. Otieno also shows sealed sodium under paraffin oil, or a photo or video of it being cut with a knife, to link back to the demo.
framework.teacherMoves: Mr. Otieno begins with a safety check: 'Goggles on before you touch anything. Show me.' He reminds learners that only the five metal samples are handled and that sodium, potassium and lithium are teacher-only. He circulates and asks each group: 'How will you make sure your scratch test is fair?' (same pressure, same tool) and 'How do you know your density reading is reliable?' (repeat the measurement). He asks one reporter per group, 5 groups in total, to read their density values aloud and posts them on the board. He then says: 'Compare your measurements with the data table. Are they close? Why might they be slightly different?' (impurities, measuring errors). WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. For Part B he says: 'Sodium sank neither in oil nor in water; it floated. Look at the density column. Which other metals would float on water? Turn to your partner.' He cold-calls 3 pairs and asks: 'What evidence in the table supports that?' He adds: 'Notice there is no melting point row for the gases, only a boiling point. Why do you think that is?' He does not explain the pattern yet; he lets learners notice first.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data collection and representation through a structured results table. Learners gather first-hand and secondary evidence on the same properties, so they can compare their own measurements with accepted values and judge reliability. Using several kinds of evidence (hands-on testing, data tables and a sodium sample or video) builds a more robust base for finding patterns than any one source alone. Reading the table for sodium, magnesium and copper links each family directly to the objects from Lesson 1.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners use a fair scratch test and record hardness as a ranking, not just 'hard' or 'soft'; (2) density calculations are correct (mass divided by volume, units g/cm3) in at least 4 of 5 groups; (3) learners correctly say which metals float on water using the 1.00 g/cm3 benchmark: Na, K and Li float, Mg, Ca, Al and the transition metals sink; (4) learners record conductivity accurately; (5) the teacher checks that every learner in each group handled or recorded something. Quick check question: 'Which has the higher melting point, K or Fe?' (Fe, 1538 C versus 63 C). Learners who struggle with the density calculation get a worked example with the Al sample.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sort the data table by chemical family using the groupings from Lesson 2: alkali metals (Li, Na, K), alkaline earth metals (Mg, Ca), transition metals (Fe, Cu, Zn), halogen (Cl2) and noble gases (Ne, Ar); Al and Pb are marked 'other metals' for now. In groups of four they identify at least two patterns: (a) within a family, e.g. Li, Na and K are all soft, low-density metals that float, with melting points of 181, 98 and 63 C, so melting point falls from Li to K; (b) across families, e.g. the alkali metals are soft, with low density and low melting points, while the transition metals are hard, dense and high melting; (c) all the listed metals conduct electricity and the three gases (Cl2, Ne, Ar) do not; (d) the gases have very low melting and boiling points. They then complete a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) statement, e.g. 'Claim: copper is better than sodium for electric wire. Evidence: copper is hard, ... conducts excellently; sodium is soft with a melting point of 98 C. Reasoning: ...' They return to their Predict-phase table and mark each prediction as supported, changed or not supported. Finally, they match properties to jobs: Al to sufuria (low density at 2.70 g/cm3, conducts heat), Cu to kettle and jiko cable (excellent conductor), Fe and Zn to mabati.
framework.teacherMoves: Mr. Otieno says: 'Using the family groupings from last lesson, sort this table. Where do the elements in the same family look alike, and where do they differ?' He gives 8 minutes of group work and circulates, asking: 'What exactly in the table makes you say that?' Pushes: 'Is it true for every element in that family?' (check against the data, e.g. Pb is soft yet very dense). WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. He cold-calls 5 groups to state one pattern each and writes them on a class chart without repeating any. He asks: 'Does the pattern hold in the other direction? If a metal is soft, is it always low density?' (No: lead is soft and heavy at 11.34 g/cm3.) He asks: 'Is melting point a good way to tell elements apart across families?' He then says: 'Return to your predictions. Which ones did the evidence change? Be ready to say why.' He cold-calls 3 learners. He introduces Mama Wanjiru's question: 'She asks why her aluminium sufuria is safe. What physical properties make aluminium suitable?' He accepts answers about low density, conducting heat and not melting at cooking temperature (660 C). He clarifies that explaining WHY the alkali metals are so soft and reactive comes in Lesson 4, so he does not give the electron explanation today.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern finding through data sorting and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning. Sorting the data by family shows learners that position in the periodic table predicts physical properties, which advances the driving question. CER forces every claim to be tied to specific numbers, so learners practise arguing from evidence rather than opinion. Revisiting predictions builds the habit of revising ideas based on data. Noting exceptions such as lead guards against overgeneralising.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners state at least two accurate patterns using numbers from the table; (2) CER statements include a claim, at least two data points and a reason that links the property to the job; (3) learners notice the exceptions (Pb soft yet dense; Al not in the four families); (4) learners mark predictions as supported or changed with a reason. Exit question on a slip: 'Name one family and two physical properties that most of its elements share.' Common error to watch for: stating that all metals are hard (Na, K, Li and Pb are soft). Teacher re-teaches with the table if more than a quarter of learners hold this idea.

framework.learnerExperience: Akinyi and Kiprop lead the DQB. Learners write new questions on sticky notes about what they have found and post them under the headings 'Properties', 'Reactivity', 'Uses' and 'Safety'. Examples: 'Why are Li, Na and K all soft and low density?' 'Why does melting point fall from Li to K?' 'Why do the gases not conduct electricity?' 'Why is copper a better conductor than lead?' 'Why did the Thika Road lamp use sodium if it is so reactive?' They also review earlier questions and mark any that the data table partly answers, e.g. 'Why does sodium float?' (density 0.97 g/cm3, below water at 1.00 g/cm3). Each learner places at least one note, and the class sorts the questions into those answerable with today's data and those that need new evidence from Lessons 4 to 7.
framework.teacherMoves: Mr. Otieno says: 'Take two minutes of silent thinking. What do you still wonder about the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle after today's data?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before learners start writing. He asks Akinyi and Kiprop to read out the new notes and place them on the board with the class. He asks: 'Which question can we already partly answer? Which needs more evidence?' He cold-calls 3 learners to explain why they placed a note under a given heading. He steers learners toward questions about reasons ('why does it follow this pattern?') and shows that these will be taken up in Lessons 4 to 6. He says: 'Let us keep our promise to the DQB. We will return to these notes in the next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking through the Driving Question Board. Moving from 'what do we see?' to 'why does it happen?' gives learners ownership of the next steps and links today's data to the driving question. Sorting questions into answered and unanswered shows how evidence builds across lessons and how new questions arise as old ones are answered.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every learner posts at least one note; (2) at least half the notes move beyond description to 'why' questions; (3) learners place notes under the correct headings and can justify the placement; (4) learners identify at least one earlier question that today's evidence has partly answered. Teacher note: record the number of 'why' questions as a gauge of readiness for Lesson 4 on alkali metals and outer electrons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add to the class Family Model, the large wall periodic table, and to their own notebook models. For each family they annotate with property labels: alkali metals (Li, Na, K): soft, low density, float on water, low melting points, conduct; alkaline earth metals (Mg, Ca): harder and denser than alkali metals, higher melting points, conduct; transition metals (Fe, Cu, Zn): hard, dense, high melting points, good conductors (Cu excellent); halogen (Cl2): greenish-yellow gas, non-conductor; noble gases (Ne, Ar): colourless gases with very low boiling points, non-conductors. Each learner draws a simple model in the notebook showing a family on the table with arrows linking its physical properties to one Kenyan job, e.g. Cu to the kettle cable, Al to the sufuria, Fe and Zn to the mabati roof. Learners add one unanswered 'why' for each family in a column labelled 'Still to explain'.
framework.teacherMoves: Mr. Otieno says: 'Our wall periodic table is our Family Model. Come and add one property label for a family, and say your evidence.' He calls 5 learners, one per family, and asks the class: 'Does the evidence support that label? Show me thumbs up or sideways.' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before votes. He asks: 'What does this model let us predict? If I give you an unknown soft metal with density 0.9 g/cm3, which family might it belong to?' He cold-calls 3 learners. He reminds them that the model is not finished: 'We still cannot explain why the families differ, or why sodium reacts so violently. Which lessons will help?' He prompts them to draw a link between family position and use, and sets the learning intention for Lesson 4: why alkali metals are so reactive.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building. Learners annotate a shared model and also draw their own, so they can see how the evidence from this lesson fits into the bigger picture. Using the model to predict an unknown element tests whether the idea of family patterns really works. Listing what the model cannot yet explain keeps learners aware that models are revised as new evidence comes in.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each learner's model correctly labels at least three families with two physical properties each; (2) the model includes at least one link from properties to a Kenyan job; (3) learners predict the likely family of an unknown soft, low-density metal as an alkali metal; (4) the 'Still to explain' column has at least one realistic question. Teacher checks notebooks while circulating. If more than a quarter of learners mislabel a family property, the teacher revisits the data table at the start of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, Mr. Otieno should consider: (1) Did learners use numbers from the table, rather than general statements, to describe patterns? (2) Did the hands-on measurements of density and conductivity match the data table closely enough for learners to trust the evidence? If not, what caused the differences? (3) Which misconceptions appeared, e.g. 'all metals are hard' or 'a heavier-looking metal always has a higher melting point', and were they resolved by the evidence? (4) Did every learner take part in the group practical, and were roles shared fairly between girls and boys? (5) Were the safety rules followed throughout, with goggles on and sodium, potassium and lithium handled only by the teacher? (6) Which DQB 'why' questions are most common, and how should Lesson 4 start from them? (7) How well did learners connect each property to a Kenyan job such as the sufuria, kettle cable or mabati roof?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We tested Mg, Al, Cu, Fe and Zn for appearance, hardness, density and conductivity, and studied a data table for Na, K, Li, Mg, Ca, Fe, Cu, Zn, Al, Pb, Cl2, Ne and Ar. Na, K and Li are soft with densities below water (0.97, 0.86, 0.53 g/cm3) and low melting points (98, 63, 181 C). Mg, Ca, Fe, Cu and Zn are denser and melt at higher temperatures. The metals conduct electricity; Cl2, Ne and Ar do not.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Elements in the same chemical family share similar physical properties, and families differ from each other. Alkali metals are soft, low in density and low melting. Transition metals are hard, dense, high melting and good conductors. Position in the periodic table helps us predict physical properties, though there are exceptions such as soft, dense lead.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Properties help explain why an element suits a job: aluminium is light and conducts heat for the sufuria, copper conducts electricity excellently for wire, and iron is strong for the mabati base. Sodium is soft, melts at only 98 C and floats, which helps us understand why it behaves differently from the metals we use for pots and wires. We still need to explain why the families differ and why sodium reacts so strongly with water, which we will investigate in Lesson 4.
