LESSONS.title: Alkali Metals: Why One Outer Electron Makes Sodium Dangerous Alone but Safe in Salt
LESSONS.aresKeywords: alkali metals, Group 1, reactivity, outer electron, lithium, sodium, potassium, balanced equation, paraffin oil, first aid, safety, phenolphthalein

slo.purpose: Learners explain why alkali metals are very reactive, and why reactivity increases down Group 1 (Li < Na < K), by linking observed reactions with water to the single outer electron that is easily lost. They write balanced equations and apply safety and first aid rules for reactive metals.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) identify the alkali metals as Group 1 elements with one outer electron (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1); (b) describe the reactions of sodium, lithium and potassium with water and air; (c) write balanced equations 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2, 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2, 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2 and 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O; (d) explain that reactivity rises down the group because the outer electron is lost more easily (Li < Na < K); (e) state safety rules and first aid for reactive metals.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (electron arrangement diagrams); planning and carrying out investigations (observing a teacher demonstration); analysing and interpreting data (ranking reactivity from evidence); constructing explanations; using mathematics (balancing equations); communicating (classroom discourse).
slo.attitudes: Love: care for self and others by observing safety and using first aid appropriately (KICD value). Self-efficacy: confidence in carrying out and interpreting investigations on reaction of metals with air and water (KICD core competency). Respect for peers' ideas during discussion. Appreciation of why safe handling matters in Kenyan labs, workshops and homes.
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 showed that sodium reacts violently with water yet salt is safe. Lesson 2 placed sodium in Group 1. Lesson 3 showed Na, K and Li are soft, low-density and low-melting. Lesson 4 gives the first reactivity evidence and the first explanation (one easily lost outer electron), answering Akinyi's DQB question 'Why is sodium dangerous?'. This idea is reused in Lesson 5 (Mg, two outer electrons, less reactive), Lesson 6 (Na + Cl2 -> NaCl) and Lesson 8.
slo.safetyNotes: TEACHER DEMONSTRATION ONLY for sodium, lithium and potassium; learners never handle them. Mr. Otieno wears goggles and a lab coat, works behind a safety screen, and uses only a pea-sized piece (about 0.1 g) of sodium, with smaller pieces of Li and K, cut under paraffin oil. Learners stay at least 2 metres back, wearing goggles. No water near stored sodium; keep metals in paraffin oil. Use a large trough, no lid, and dispose of residues as the teacher directs (do not tip leftover metal in the sink). Keep a bucket of dry sand, a first aid kit and water source ready. First aid: for skin contact, brush off any metal and flood with running water for at least 10 minutes; for eye splashes, rinse with clean water for 10 minutes and get medical help; report every injury. Phenolphthalein and alkaline solutions are irritants, so wear goggles when handling them.

LESSONS.overview: Mr. Otieno's Kisumu class returns to the sodium puzzle from Lesson 1. Learners first predict how lithium, sodium and potassium will compare in water and why. They then watch a teacher demonstration behind a safety screen and record observations in a table (floating, fizzing, speed, melting, flame, colour with phenolphthalein). Next they rank reactivity (Li < Na < K), draw the electron arrangements (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1) and explain with the idea that an atom with one outer electron loses it easily, and more easily as the outer electron is further from the nucleus. They write and balance equations and rehearse safety and first aid rules. Akinyi and Kiprop update the Driving Question Board (Properties, Reactivity, Uses, Safety) and the class family model, adding the Group 1 reactivity arrow. The lesson ends with a link back to the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle: sodium is dangerous alone because it loses its outer electron so easily, so we must understand it before judging where it is safe.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the sodium demo from Lesson 1 and Group 1 from Lesson 2. Individually, in 3 minutes, each writes a prediction on a sticky note or in their notebook: 'If a pea-sized piece of lithium, sodium and potassium each go into water, what will happen, and which will react fastest? Why?' They draw a quick sketch of the three troughs. In pairs they compare predictions, then add one reason, using the soft, low-density, low-melting properties from Lesson 3 (e.g. 'they float because density is below 1.00 g/cm3').
framework.teacherMoves: Display the three symbols and Z (Li 3, Na 11, K 19) and the Group 1 column on the wall periodic table. Say: 'Remember Mama Wanjiru's question: her aluminium sufuria is safe, but sodium reacts violently with water. Today we compare three cousins in Group 1. Before I show anything, what do you think will happen? Write your prediction first.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which one do you think will be the most dramatic, and what is your reason?' Cold-call 4 learners from different parts of the room, no hands up, and record each prediction on the board in two columns: 'Prediction' and 'Reason'. Do not say who is right. Say: 'Keep your note. We will test it in a few minutes.' Circulate and note misconceptions such as 'heavier means faster' or 'the metal burns in the water because water is hot'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas through commit-and-compare predictions. Writing a prediction with a reason before evidence makes learners' mental models visible, creates a personal stake in the demonstration, and lets them later revise their own thinking rather than just receive an answer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) at least 80% of learners write a prediction AND a reason; (2) listen for use of Lesson 3 ideas (soft, low density, floats) and Lesson 2 ideas (same group, so similar). Tally how many predict K fastest versus Li fastest. Record misconceptions on a clipboard checklist to address in the Explain phase. Learners who give only a prediction without a reason get a prompt: 'What makes you think so?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit at least 2 metres back, wearing goggles, behind the safety screen. They watch Mr. Otieno (a) cut a fresh piece of sodium under paraffin oil and note the shiny surface that quickly dulls in air, and (b) drop a pea-sized piece of sodium, then lithium, then potassium (if available) into separate troughs of water with phenolphthalein. In groups of 4 they complete an observation table: metal, floats/sinks, fizzing (slow/fast/very fast), melts into a ball (yes/no), flame colour, solution colour with phenolphthalein. Roles: observer 1 (movement), observer 2 (sound and fizz), recorder, timer who estimates seconds until the reaction slows. Learners see: Li slow fizz; Na fast fizz, melts and darts about, solution turns pink; K very fast, lilac flame. If K or Li are not available, learners use the teacher's described reference data card for these two and clearly mark it as 'secondary data' in the table. After the demo, groups add a note on the metal stored under paraffin oil and why (no air, no water).
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting, rehearse safety: 'Goggles on. Everyone stays behind the line. No one touches the metals. Why do we use only a pea-sized piece?' Cold-call 2 learners for answers. Cut sodium under oil with a knife, show the shiny surface for 5 seconds, and ask: 'What do you notice about the cut surface and what do you think happens to it in air?' WAIT 10-15 seconds, cold-call 2 learners. Before each drop ask: 'Based on your prediction, what will you watch for?' Drop lithium first, then sodium, then potassium, pausing 30 seconds between each to let learners record. After each, ask the recorder group to read their observation aloud. Say: 'Describe only what you SEE and HEAR, not why yet.' Add a few drops of phenolphthalein to each trough afterwards and ask: 'What does the pink colour tell us about the solution?' WAIT 10 seconds; cold-call 2 learners and confirm that an alkali has formed. Point to the bubbles: 'A gas is made. We will find out what it is in the Explain phase.' If any metal remains, place it in the dry sand or dispose as the teacher directs, and state this aloud as modelling safe practice. Do not hurry or add larger pieces.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation with data tables (Science and Engineering Practice: Planning and carrying out investigations). Separating observation from explanation keeps learners focused on evidence, and the common table lets groups compare the same variables across three metals so a pattern (Li < Na < K) can emerge from data rather than from the teacher's statement.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: tables are completed for all three metals with specific descriptive words (not just 'it reacted'); learners record the pink colour and link it to an alkali; at least one entry per group notes that the metals float (link to density below 1.00 g/cm3). Check that groups rank the three metals by speed and violence of reaction. Teacher checks goggles on and distance kept for every learner throughout. Ask one group member to read their table; correct vague statements with 'Can you describe what you saw in more detail?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their data to rank reactivity: Li < Na < K. They draw electron arrangements in their notebooks and on the board: Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1, and circle the single outer electron in each. In groups they build a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) statement: 'Alkali metals are very reactive because ...' and 'Potassium is more reactive than sodium because ...' using the idea that each atom loses its outer electron easily, and the outer electron in K is further from the nucleus (more shells) so is lost more easily. They then write word equations and balance symbol equations: 2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2; 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2; and 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O (the dulling of cut sodium in air). They identify the gas as hydrogen, H2, and explain why the solution turned pink (alkali: hydroxide formed). They also complete a safety and first aid card: rules (goggles, small quantities, never touch with bare hands, store under paraffin oil, no water near stored sodium, dispose as directed) and first aid steps for skin, eye and fire situations, and link these to the earlier sodium risk in Lesson 1. Finally they compare their original predictions with the evidence and write one sentence: 'My prediction was ... The evidence showed ... so I now think ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Return to the predictions board: 'Look at your sticky note. Whose prediction matched? What do you want to change?' Cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'Which metal was the most reactive? What evidence from your table shows that?' WAIT 10-15 seconds, cold-call 3 groups, and write the order Li < Na < K on the board. Draw the three atoms on the board and ask: 'What is the same about all three? What is different?' WAIT 10 seconds. Guide: all have one outer electron; K has more shells. Ask: 'If an atom has just one electron on the outside, what might it want to do with it?' WAIT 15 seconds; cold-call 2 learners. Introduce only the idea that the metal atom LOSES its outer electron (do not teach ionic bonding in detail, ion formulas, or electronegativity). Say: 'The further the outer electron is from the nucleus, the easier it is to lose, so reactivity goes up the way we saw: Li, then Na, then K.' Model balancing 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 on the board by counting atoms on each side aloud, then let learners balance the Li and K equations in pairs while you circulate. Cold-call 3 pairs to write their balanced equations on the board; ask the class to check each by counting atoms. Ask: 'Is this equation balanced? How do you know?' Address misconceptions such as 'sodium burns the water' or 'bigger atom, slower reaction'. Run a safety card activity: 'Mr. Otieno says never touch sodium with bare hands. Use the first aid steps to explain why and what you would do if a splash reached your arm.' Cold-call 4 learners across the room, then confirm the steps. Close by linking back: 'Sodium is dangerous alone because its one outer electron is lost so readily. That is also why, once combined, as in salt on Mama Wanjiru's ugali, it is a very different substance. We will explore that with chlorine in Lesson 6.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with model-based explanation (Science and Engineering Practices: Constructing explanations; Developing and using models; Using mathematics). Learners must link their own observed evidence to an atomic-level model of outer electrons, which makes the invisible cause of reactivity concrete and turns balanced equations into a record of what happens rather than a memorised routine. Revisiting predictions supports conceptual change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) correct ranking Li < Na < K supported by at least two pieces of evidence from the table; (2) electron arrangements written correctly (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1) with the outer electron circled; (3) CER statements include the single outer electron AND the idea that it is lost easily; (4) at least 75% of pairs balance all three water equations correctly; (5) learners name H2 and NaOH/LiOH/KOH correctly; (6) safety card correctly lists at least four rules and the first aid steps. Exit check: on a slip, 'Why is potassium more reactive than lithium?' Learners who say only 'because it is bigger' are given the prompt 'What does that mean for the outer electron?'.

framework.learnerExperience: Akinyi and Kiprop lead the DQB update. In their groups, learners write new questions and answers on sticky notes, sorting them into the DQB categories Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety. They move Akinyi's question 'Why is sodium dangerous?' to 'partly answered' with a note: 'one outer electron, lost very easily'. They add new questions such as 'Why does magnesium not react with cold water like sodium?', 'Why is sodium safe in salt?', 'Why do street lamps along Thika Road glow yellow?' and 'What do we do if sodium touches skin?'. Each learner contributes at least one note, and the class decides which questions the next lesson (Lesson 5) can address.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Akinyi and Kiprop, please read the questions on the board that we can now partly answer.' Give groups 4 minutes to write at least 2 new questions each. Ask: 'Which questions did today's evidence help us answer, and which new ones did it raise?' WAIT 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 groups to place one note and explain the category chosen. Prompt: 'Which new question links to the periodic table position?' Point out that questions on Mg and halogens will be tackled in Lessons 5 and 6 without answering them yet. Ensure Safety notes receive attention: 'Who can add a question or a rule about first aid?' Photograph or copy the DQB for the offline record.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding (question-driven learning). Sorting questions into categories shows learners how today's evidence answers some questions, narrows others and generates new ones, so learning feels purposeful and connected to the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: every learner contributes at least one question or answer note; notes are placed in suitable categories; at least two new questions show reasoning from today's evidence (for example comparing Na with Mg, or asking why sodium in salt is safe). Teacher checks the Safety category contains at least one first aid question. Note learners whose questions are only factual recall and encourage 'why' or 'how' questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update the class family model, the large wall periodic table. They add to Group 1: the label 'Alkali metals: 1 outer electron', the electron arrangements Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1, and an arrow down the group labelled 'reactivity increases: Li < Na < K'. They add a small note 'very reactive, stored under paraffin oil, teacher demo only' and the key equation 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. In their notebooks, each learner revises their own model of 'Why is sodium dangerous alone?' with a labelled diagram: sodium atom 2,8,1, the outer electron leaving, water, and hydrogen gas bubbles. They finish with a one-sentence link: 'Because sodium atoms lose their single outer electron very easily, ... so sodium is stored under paraffin oil and ... but I still need to find out why salt (NaCl) is safe.' They complete the summary table prompt (observed, learned, explained).
framework.teacherMoves: Invite two learners to add the labels and arrow to the wall periodic table while the class checks: 'Does this match our evidence? Is the arrow in the right direction?' WAIT 10 seconds. Ask: 'Predict: where would you place rubidium below potassium? What reactivity would you expect and why?' Cold-call 2 learners (extension, no equipment). Ask: 'What is still missing from our model?' WAIT 10-15 seconds; cold-call 3 learners; guide toward: why Mg is different (Lesson 5), why sodium combined with chlorine is safe (Lesson 6), why sodium vapour glows yellow. Say: 'Keep your model; we will keep revising it.' Collect notebook diagrams at the door and check for the outer electron and the hydrogen gas. For homework, ask learners to find two Kenyan places where reactive metals must be stored or handled carefully (for example school labs or jua kali workshops in Gikomba) and write one safety rule for each.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (Science and Engineering Practice: Developing and using models). Adding the Group 1 reactivity trend and electron arrangements to a shared model lets learners see that position in the periodic table predicts behaviour, which is the central idea for choosing the right element for the right job, and gives a concrete anchor for later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: wall model annotations are accurate (1 outer electron, arrow direction, correct electron arrangements); individual notebook diagrams show the sodium atom with the outer electron leaving, the hydrogen gas and the correct balanced equation; learners can state a limit of the model (it does not yet explain why salt is safe or why Mg is less reactive). Score each diagram: electron shown, trend shown, equation balanced, safety named. Provide extra support for learners missing two or more.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on these questions: (1) Did every learner stay behind the safety line and wear goggles, and were safety rules followed without reminders? (2) How many learners moved from predicting by 'size or weight' to explaining by 'outer electron lost more easily', and what evidence from CER statements shows this? (3) Which learners struggled to balance 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 and what helped (counting atoms aloud, drawing atoms)? (4) Did the observation table help learners separate what they saw from why it happened? (5) If potassium or lithium was unavailable, did the secondary data card give learners enough evidence to rank Li < Na < K? (6) Did the DQB capture new 'why' questions, and are the Lesson 5 and Lesson 6 questions ready? Note any misconceptions (for example that sodium 'burns' water, or that a bigger atom is less reactive) to revisit at the start of Lesson 5.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Lithium fizzes slowly in water, sodium fizzes fast, melts into a ball and darts about, and potassium reacts very fast with a lilac flame. All three float and the solution turns pink with phenolphthalein. Freshly cut sodium is shiny but quickly dulls in air. (Record what you saw and heard in your own words.)
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Alkali metals (Group 1) have one outer electron (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1). Reactivity increases down the group: Li < Na < K. They react with water to form an alkali (hydroxide) and hydrogen gas, and with oxygen in air. They must be stored under paraffin oil, handled only by the teacher, and any contact with skin or eyes needs immediate flushing with running water.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Alkali metals are very reactive because each atom has a single outer electron that is lost very easily. Down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases. This is why sodium reacts violently with water (2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2) and is dangerous alone, which links to the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle. We still need to explain why sodium combined as salt is safe.

LESSONS.title: Alkaline Earth Metals: Is Magnesium as Dangerous as Sodium?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: alkaline earth metals, magnesium, Group 2, two outer electrons, reactivity, burning in air, dilute hydrochloric acid, balanced equation, MgO, reactivity order

slo.purpose: Learners compare how magnesium reacts with air, water and dilute acid, relate its lower reactivity to its two outer electrons, write balanced equations for Mg, and use the evidence to revise the class family model and explain why Mg and Na are suited to different jobs in the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) investigate the physical and chemical properties of selected elements of the periodic table (magnesium with air, water and dilute acid); (b) state that alkaline earth metals (Group 2: Be, Mg, Ca) have two outer electrons (Mg 2,8,2); (c) explain that magnesium is less reactive than sodium (order K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg) even though both lose outer electrons; (d) write balanced equations 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO and Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2; (e) appreciate the uses of the elements of the periodic table in day-to-day life.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (revising the class family model); planning and carrying out investigations (air, water and acid tests with Mg ribbon); analysing and interpreting data (ranking reactivity from observations); constructing explanations; using mathematics (balancing atoms); core competency: Self-efficacy as the learner carries out activities to investigate the reaction of magnesium with air and dilute acids.
slo.attitudes: Love: learners take care of self and others by observing safety when investigating the elements and by knowing where the first aid kit is. Respect: learners listen to and build on group members' ideas. Responsibility: learners handle materials and waste as directed. PCI: Safety and security.
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 4 showed that alkali metals are very reactive because each has one easily lost outer electron. Here learners test a Group 2 metal and find it far less violent than sodium. This gives the first evidence that reactivity differs between families and that outer electrons alone do not decide it. It also begins to answer Akinyi's DQB question on why sodium is dangerous, and prepares Lesson 6 (halogens and noble gases).
slo.safetyNotes: Goggles on for all learners at all times. Mg ribbon pieces about 2 cm only. Teacher demonstrates the burning of Mg in air with a tongs, behind a safety screen, and learners must NOT look directly at the bright white flame (view through a gap in fingers or at an angle, or use a piece of dark glass). Dilute HCl about 0.5 mol/dm3 only: wash splashes with plenty of running water; first aid kit and water available. Hydrogen gas is flammable: no naked flame near the acid test tubes except the teacher's supervised pop test. Learners do not handle sodium, potassium or lithium; any reference to Na is from Lesson 1 and 4 evidence. Dispose of residues as directed by the teacher.

LESSONS.overview: Mr. Otieno in Kisumu reminds the class of the sodium demo and the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle. Akinyi asks: 'If sodium is so dangerous, are all metals like that?' Learners predict how magnesium ribbon will behave compared with sodium. They then gather evidence in groups: Mg ribbon in cold water, Mg ribbon in dilute HCl, and a teacher demonstration of Mg burning in air. They compare with the Lesson 4 sodium evidence and the Lesson 3 data (Mg density 1.74 g/cm3, melting 650 C versus Na 0.97 g/cm3, 98 C). In the Explain phase they use the electron arrangements Na 2,8,1 and Mg 2,8,2 to build explanations, write and balance 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO and Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, and rank K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg. They add new questions to the DQB and revise the class family model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown a 5 cm piece of shiny Mg ribbon, beside a photo of the sodium demo from Lesson 1. Individually (3 minutes) on a prediction sheet they write: (1) what will happen if Mg ribbon goes in cold water, (2) what will happen in dilute HCl, (3) what will happen if it is heated in air, and (4) whether Mg will be more or less reactive than Na, with a reason using what they know about outer electrons from Lesson 4. They draw a quick sketch of what they expect to see in the water test. Then they pair-share and mark each prediction with a confidence level (sure / not sure).
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the ribbon and say: 'Remember Mr. Otieno's sodium fizzing across the trough on Thika Road day. Magnesium sits next to sodium in the periodic table. Will it do the same? Write your prediction first, no talking.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before anyone speaks. Walk the room and note 4 different predictions. Cold-call 3 learners (not volunteers) to share one prediction and its reason. Say: 'Thank you. I am not telling you who is right. We will let the evidence decide.' Write 2 competing predictions on the board. Point out that the magnesium used in school labs is also in some ordinary things, such as flash bulbs in older cameras and in some antacid tablets, so learners see it is not always dangerous.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with confidence rating (commitment before evidence): writing a prediction and a reason makes learners' current model visible and gives them a stake in the outcome. When evidence later contradicts a prediction, the conflict drives revision of the model, not just memorising a result.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) at least 3 of 4 prediction items completed with a reason; (b) whether the learner links reactivity to outer electrons or just guesses ('because it is a metal'); (c) at least 5 of 8 groups include a comparison with Na. Record the common misconception that 'all metals next to sodium must fizz in water' to revisit in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 (roles: reader, handler, recorder, reporter) wearing goggles do Station A and Station B for 12 minutes each, then watch the demo. Station A (cold water): clean a 2 cm piece of Mg ribbon with sandpaper, drop it into a test tube of cold water, observe for 3 minutes, then add 2 drops of phenolphthalein; record bubbles, colour and whether the ribbon moves or melts. Station B (dilute acid): place a 2 cm clean Mg ribbon in a test tube with 5 cm3 of dilute HCl; record bubbling speed, temperature change by feeling the outside of the tube, and what happens to the ribbon. The teacher then tests the gas with a lighted splint (pop test) while learners watch. Demonstration C (air): Mr. Otieno holds a 3 cm Mg ribbon in tongs and ignites it behind a screen; learners watch the bright white flame from an angle and note the white powder (MgO) left behind. Each group fills an observation table with columns: test, what we saw, did it react (fast / slow / none). They also look at the Lesson 3 data table to recall Mg density 1.74 g/cm3 (sinks in water) and melting point 650 C, compared with Na 0.97 g/cm3 and 98 C.
framework.teacherMoves: Brief the class: 'Goggles on. Two centimetres only. Describe what you SEE, not what you think should happen.' Circulate with a checklist and ask each group: 'What evidence tells you whether a reaction is happening?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before prompting. At Station A, if learners report 'nothing', say: 'Is nothing a result? Look closely at the ribbon surface for tiny bubbles. Compare with the sodium video.' Before the demo say: 'Do not stare at the flame. Look sideways.' After the pop test ask 2 cold-called learners: 'What gas gives a pop with a lighted splint?' Ensure learners notice that Mg sinks in water (density 1.74 g/cm3) while Na floated. Remind the class that sodium, potassium and lithium are shown only by the teacher and are never handled by learners. Keep the first aid kit visible and name its location.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation table with 'evidence vs inference' columns: learners record only what they saw (bubbles, flame colour, white powder) in one column and what they think it means in another. This separates observation from interpretation and helps them build claims from evidence, which they will use in the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) goggles on and 2 cm ribbon used by 100% of groups; (b) tables record at least 3 reactions with appropriate descriptors (no visible reaction in cold water; slow-to-steady bubbles in HCl; bright white flame in air); (c) at least 6 of 8 groups correctly name the pop-test gas as hydrogen; (d) groups distinguish observation from inference in their table. Teacher notes groups that write 'it reacted violently', which signals a Na-based assumption to correct.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work first in groups, then as a class. Step 1 (10 minutes): groups rank the reactions they saw from least to most vigorous and compare with the Lesson 4 sodium evidence (Na fast fizz and melts in water; Mg no visible reaction in cold water). Step 2: using the electron arrangements Na 2,8,1 and Mg 2,8,2, groups discuss: 'Both lose outer electrons, so why is Mg less reactive?' Guiding idea to build on: Mg has two outer electrons to lose, and the metal is denser and has a higher melting point (Lesson 3 data), so it holds on more strongly than Na and reacts less readily. Step 3: write and balance equations in their notebooks: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO; Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2; and compare with 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 and 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O. Learners count atoms on each side for every equation and show it in a small atom-count table. Step 4: place Na, Mg, Li, K, Ca in order of reactivity: K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg, justifying each position from the evidence. Step 5: relate to the phenomenon: Why is Mg safe to handle as a ribbon while Na must be kept under paraffin oil? Which element would be unsuitable for a sufuria and why?
framework.teacherMoves: Pose: 'Sodium and magnesium both lose outer electrons. Sodium fizzes in cold water, magnesium does not. What does that tell us about how easily each loses electrons?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to give a claim, then ask 2 others: 'Do you agree? What evidence supports that?' Model balancing 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO on the board: write the unbalanced Mg + O2 -> MgO, count Mg and O on each side (1 Mg, 2 O on left; 1 Mg, 1 O on right), then add a coefficient 2 before MgO and then 2 before Mg. Then release groups to balance Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2 themselves, checking H and Cl. Check understanding: 'If you change the small number in a formula, what happens to the substance? So what can we change?' (only coefficients). Address the Predict-phase misconception that all metals near sodium behave like sodium. Do not introduce ions, ionic bonding or electronegativity; keep the explanation at 'the metal atom loses its outer electrons'. Link back: 'Why do we cook ugali in aluminium and not in Mg-rich or sodium pots? Think about reactivity and the evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a rank-and-justify task: learners state a claim (Mg is less reactive than Na), cite evidence (no reaction in cold water, slower bubbles in acid, higher melting point, two outer electrons), and give reasoning linking electrons to reactivity. Balancing equations with atom-count tables turns a procedure into a conservation-of-atoms argument.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (a) at least 80% of groups write a CER with all three parts, citing at least two pieces of evidence; (b) learners correctly balance 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO and Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2 with atom counts (exit slip of 3 items: balance Mg + O2 -> MgO; state the number of outer electrons in Mg; order Na, Mg, K by reactivity); (c) learners correctly order K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg; (d) at least 70% correctly state that Mg has 2 outer electrons (2,8,2). Common errors to note: changing subscripts to balance; writing MgO2; saying Mg is unreactive rather than less reactive than Na.

framework.learnerExperience: Akinyi and Kiprop, the DQB keepers, invite groups to revisit the board. Each learner (a) finds one earlier question that this lesson helps answer (for example Akinyi's 'Why is sodium dangerous?') and writes a short evidence note on a sticky note, and (b) writes one new question on a different-coloured sticky note (for example 'Why does Ca react less than Na but still fizz?', 'Is magnesium used in anything like the sufuria?', 'What makes chlorine different?'). Notes are sorted into the four categories: Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety. The class then chooses 2 new questions to follow up in Lessons 6 and 7.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk to the DQB. Find a question we can now partly answer. Stick your evidence next to it, in your own words.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing (WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before sharing). Cold-call 3 learners to read a new question aloud and ask the class: 'Which category does this belong in, and why?' Ask Kiprop to read one question about the yellow Thika Road lamps and signal that Lesson 6 will return to it. Move questions that are already answered to an 'Answered so far' strip, and mark those that need more evidence with a question mark. Praise questions that can be tested.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record of understanding: sorting questions into categories and attaching evidence shows learners how their knowledge grows and identifies gaps, keeping the investigation learner-driven and connected to the anchoring puzzle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (a) every learner adds at least one evidence note or new question; (b) at least 60% of new questions are testable and linked to reactivity, family position or use; (c) notes are placed in the correct category by at least 80% of learners; (d) at least 5 learners link their note to the outer-electron idea. Teacher photographs the DQB to track which questions remain open.

framework.learnerExperience: Kiprop and Akinyi lead the revision of the Class Family Model (wall periodic table). Learners annotate: (1) Group 2 column (Be, Mg, Ca) with 'two outer electrons' and 'less reactive than Group 1 in the same period'; (2) a note on Mg: burns with a bright white flame to form MgO, no visible reaction with cold water, reacts with dilute HCl giving H2; (3) a reactivity arrow K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg; (4) the two balanced equations. Each group then sketches a revised model on a sheet: Mg 2,8,2 and Na 2,8,1 shown as shell diagrams with the outer electrons circled, and a caption starting 'Magnesium is less reactive than sodium because...'. Finally learners write a 3-line answer to the lesson question: 'Is magnesium as dangerous as sodium? What does that suggest about choosing an element for a job?' and list one open question about the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model last lesson said alkali metals are reactive because of one outer electron. What must we add or change after meeting magnesium?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for one revision each. Ask: 'What stays the same, what changes?' (family behaviour is linked to outer electrons, but the number and strength of holding matter, so position in the table predicts how reactive an element is). Push for the idea that position in the periodic table helps predict behaviour. Collect the revised models and exit slips. Remind learners of safety: no tasting or removing materials from the lab, wash hands, and dispose of residues as directed. Preview Lesson 6: halogens and noble gases, including chlorine in Mombasa water and neon signs.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners add new evidence to a shared model and explicitly state what they are changing and why. Drawing shell diagrams and writing a 'because' caption connects particle-level structure to observed behaviour, supporting prediction of other elements' behaviour from their position.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (a) at least 80% of revised models show Mg 2,8,2 with two circled outer electrons and Na 2,8,1 with one; (b) captions include a causal 'because'; (c) the 3-line answer states that Mg is less reactive than Na and gives evidence; (d) at least 60% of learners note that reactivity affects suitability for a job; (e) the class model is updated with the reactivity arrow and both balanced equations.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did learners separate observation from inference at the stations? Which prediction misconception (all metals near sodium fizz in water) persisted and in how many groups? Did the safety routines (goggles, 2 cm ribbon, not looking at the flame) hold? How many learners could balance both equations unaided, and what did the errors reveal (changing subscripts, MgO2)? Did the explanation stay at 'loses outer electrons' without drifting into ionic bonding? Which DQB questions should Lessons 6 and 7 target? What would you change in the grouping, timing or use of the Lesson 3 density and melting point data?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Magnesium ribbon showed no visible reaction in cold water, gave steady bubbles of hydrogen gas in dilute HCl (pop test positive), and burned with a bright white flame in air leaving white MgO powder. Sodium, by comparison, fizzes fast in water and melts.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Alkaline earth metals (Group 2) have two outer electrons (Mg 2,8,2). Magnesium is less reactive than sodium. The reactivity order is K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg. Equations are balanced by adjusting coefficients so atoms are conserved.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Both sodium and magnesium react by losing outer electrons, but magnesium reacts less readily, shown by no cold-water reaction and slower reaction with acid. Its position in the periodic table lets us predict this: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO and Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. So reactivity helps decide which element suits which job and how safely it can be handled.

LESSONS.title: Halogens and Noble Gases: Why Chlorine Cleans Mombasa Water and Neon Lights the Sign
LESSONS.aresKeywords: halogens, chlorine, Group 17, noble gases, Group 18, outer electrons, full outer shell, water treatment, 0.5 mg/L, neon, argon, unreactive, sodium chloride

slo.purpose: To use evidence from chlorine's reactions (teacher demonstration, video and simulation) and noble gas data to explain how outer electrons make halogens reactive, why a tiny dose of chlorine makes Mombasa and Nairobi water safe, and why noble gases are unreactive and suited to signs and lighting.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) state that halogens (Group 17) have 7 outer electrons and are reactive non-metals (Cl 2,8,7); (b) describe chlorine as a greenish-yellow, toxic gas that reacts with sodium: 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl; (c) explain that chlorine at about 0.5 mg/L kills the bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid, and that only a small safe dose is used; (d) state that noble gases (Group 18) have full outer shells (Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8; He 2) and are therefore unreactive; (e) outline the uses of neon in signs and relate the unreactive nature of noble gases to their applications.
slo.skills: Predicting from electron arrangements; interpreting a data table (boiling points, state, electrical conduction); developing and using models (annotating the class family model); constructing explanations from evidence; writing and balancing a chemical equation; communicating in group discussion (SEP: Analysing and interpreting data; Developing and using models; Constructing explanations).
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the uses of the elements of the periodic table in day-to-day life; show care for self and others by observing safety around toxic gases and reactive metals (value: Love); respect others' opinions during discussion (value: Respect); take responsibility for safe use of digital devices when watching the simulation (value: Responsibility). Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration; Digital literacy; Self-efficacy. PCIs: Road safety (properties of elements that make them suitable for illuminating roads); Safety and security; Health (safe drinking water).
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 4 and 5 showed that reactivity depends on outer electrons (alkali metals lose 1 easily; magnesium has 2 and is less reactive). Lesson 6 uses Group 17 and Group 18 to complete the picture: chlorine is reactive because it is one electron short of a full outer shell, yet a tiny dose makes Mombasa water safe, while noble gases with full shells are unreactive and so suit signs and lamps. This closes two threads from Lesson 1 (Mombasa chlorinated water and the street lamp) and prepares for Lesson 7 (transition metals) and Lesson 8 (choosing the right element for the job).
slo.safetyNotes: Chlorine gas is toxic: learners do NOT handle chlorine. Mr. Otieno-style teacher demonstration only, in a fume cupboard or in a well-ventilated area outdoors behind a safety screen, using a very small amount; if no safe set-up is available, use the video and simulation instead. Teacher wears goggles and lab coat; learners stay at least 2 m back with goggles on. Sodium is never handled by learners and is kept under paraffin oil; keep water away from stored sodium. Anyone feeling throat irritation moves to fresh air immediately and the teacher uses the first aid kit. Dispose of residues as directed by the teacher. Never mix household bleach (e.g., Jik) with any acid or other cleaner.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru in Mombasa cooks ugali in an aluminium sufuria and asks: why is her tap water safe when chlorine as a gas is poisonous? Learners start by predicting what chlorine will do to sodium and why a lamp gas such as neon does nothing at all. They gather evidence from a teacher demonstration or video of chlorine (greenish-yellow gas, reacting with sodium to make salt, 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl), the water-treatment data (about 0.5 mg/L at the Mombasa water works), and a data table of Ne and Ar electron arrangements and boiling points. They then explain reactivity in terms of outer electrons (Cl needs one more; Ne and Ar already have a full outer shell), post and sort new questions on the Driving Question Board, and annotate the class family model. This lesson connects the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle back to the periodic table: position predicts behaviour, and behaviour decides the job.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 12 min) Learners look at two items on the front bench: a clear bottle of Mombasa/Nairobi-style treated tap water and a photo of a neon sign next to a photo of a Thika Road sodium lamp. Individually, in their notebooks, they answer: (1) Chlorine atoms have 7 outer electrons (Cl 2,8,7). Predict what chlorine will do when it meets sodium (2,8,1), and draw a quick sketch of the outer electrons. (2) Neon has the arrangement 2,8 and argon 2,8,8. Predict whether neon will react with sodium, and why or why not. (3) Mama Wanjiru asks why chlorine gas is poisonous but her tap water is safe: write one idea. Learners then compare ideas with a partner and post one prediction on a sticky note.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Mama Wanjiru cooks ugali in her sufuria in Mombasa. She says chlorine is poisonous, so why is it in her tap water? Before I show you anything, write what you think." Hold up the electron arrangements on the board (Na 2,8,1; Cl 2,8,7; Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8). Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before calling on anyone. Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) to share a prediction, and ask each: "What in the electron arrangement made you say that?" Do not say who is right. Record 3-4 predictions on the board under the headings 'Chlorine + sodium', 'Neon + sodium' and 'Safe water'. Remind learners of Lesson 4 (alkali metals lose their one outer electron easily) and Lesson 5 (Mg has two outer electrons and is less reactive).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (commit to a prediction with reasoning): writing a prediction tied to electron arrangement makes learners' existing ideas about outer electrons visible and creates a reason to look at the evidence. Revisiting predictions later in the lesson lets them see their own thinking change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (a) refer to outer electrons rather than just 'chlorine is bad', (b) link sodium's behaviour from Lesson 4 to the new prediction, (c) connect 'full shell' to 'does not react' in the neon prediction. Tally on the board how many predict that neon reacts and how many that it does not. Note common ideas such as 'chlorine in water must be harmful' or 'all gases react' for use in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 25 min) Learners gather evidence in three stations or segments and record in a three-column table (What I observed / What it shows about outer electrons / Link to the puzzle). Segment A (8 min): Teacher demonstration (or video) of chlorine: greenish-yellow gas in a gas jar; a small heated piece of sodium lowered into chlorine burns with a bright yellow flame, forming white solid NaCl. Learners note colour, smell warning (not smelled), flame and product, then copy the equation 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl and count atoms on both sides to check it balances. Segment B (8 min): In groups of 4, learners study a data card: Mombasa water works adds about 0.5 mg of free chlorine per litre, which kills the bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid; chlorine gas at high concentration is toxic, so only a small safe dose is used. They calculate how much chlorine is needed for a 20 litre jerrican (0.5 mg/L x 20 L = 10 mg) and for a 1,000 litre tank (500 mg), and discuss why dose matters. Segment C (9 min): Learners analyse a table: Ne colourless gas, 2,8, boils at -246 C, non-conductor; Ar colourless gas, 2,8,8, boils at -186 C, non-conductor; Cl2 greenish-yellow gas, 2,8,7, boils at -34 C. They also use a short simulation (or video) of neon in a glass tube glowing red-orange when electricity passes through, and compare with the Thika Road sodium lamp's yellow-orange light. They note that neon and argon were not changed by the electricity and did not react with anything.
framework.teacherMoves: For Segment A, stand behind the safety screen with goggles and lab coat; say: "Goggles on. Everyone stays behind the line. Chlorine is toxic, so I do the demonstration and you do the observing." If not safe to demonstrate, play the video and say: "Watch for three things: the colour of the gas, the flame, and the colour of the product." Ask: "What happened to the sodium? What is the white solid? Where have we met it?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before calling on a learner; cold-call 3 learners. Prompt: "Sodium lost its one outer electron in Lesson 4. Where might that electron have gone?" (without formal ionic bonding detail: say only that the sodium atom gives up its outer electron and chlorine takes one). For Segment B, circulate and ask each group: "If 0.5 mg/L is safe and kills bacteria, what would happen if the dose were 100 times bigger?" For Segment C, ask: "What pattern do you see between the electron arrangements of Ne and Ar and their behaviour?" Cold-call 4 groups to share one pattern each. Check that groups compute 10 mg and 500 mg correctly and that the equation balances (2 Na, 2 Cl on each side).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence table with data analysis (Analysing and interpreting data): learners separate what they saw from what it means and link each observation to outer electrons. Using numbers (0.5 mg/L, boiling points) turns the phenomenon into measurable evidence rather than opinion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners (a) record at least three observations accurately (greenish-yellow gas, bright yellow flame, white solid NaCl); (b) balance 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl with 2 Na and 2 Cl on each side; (c) calculate 10 mg for 20 L and 500 mg for 1,000 L; (d) note that Ne and Ar are gases with very low boiling points that do not conduct or react. Use a thumbs-up/sideways check: 'Can you say in one sentence why chlorine is reactive?' and note learners who need support.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 20 min) In groups of 4, learners build a written explanation using a claim-evidence-reasoning frame to answer two linked questions: (1) Why is chlorine reactive, and why can a tiny dose of 0.5 mg/L make Mombasa water safe even though chlorine gas is toxic? (2) Why are neon and argon unreactive, and why does that suit them for signs and lamps? They must use: Cl 2,8,7 (7 outer electrons, one short of a full shell of 8); Na 2,8,1 (one outer electron easily lost); Ne 2,8 and Ar 2,8,8 (full outer shells, nothing to gain or lose); the equation 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl; and the dose data. They also explain the sodium-lamp puzzle: the Thika Road sodium vapour lamp gives yellow light, neon signs glow red-orange, and why both are chosen for the job (neon is unreactive and so safe and stable inside a sealed glass tube; sodium is used as a vapour for its yellow light). Groups then revisit their predictions from the Predict phase, mark each as supported or not supported, and correct it. Finally, they use the gallery walk: groups swap explanations and give one star and one question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use the frame: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning. Your reasoning must mention outer electrons." Provide the sentence starters: "Chlorine is reactive because its atoms have ___ outer electrons, so they ___." and "Neon is unreactive because ___." Circulate and ask: "Why does the same chlorine that kills bacteria at 0.5 mg/L harm people at high concentration?" and "Is a gas that does not react the same as a gas that is useless? Where in Kenya do we use it?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 5 learners from different groups to read a claim aloud, and ask a different group to add evidence. Address misconceptions: (i) 'chlorine in tap water is the same as chlorine gas leaking' (clarify dose: 0.5 mg/L is a tiny safe amount); (ii) 'noble gases are unreactive because they are cold' (clarify full outer shell); (iii) 'the sodium lamp contains neon' (sodium vapour lamp uses sodium). Do not introduce ionic bonding detail, ion formulas or electronegativity: say only that the sodium atom gives up its outer electron and the chlorine atom takes one, giving the stable compound NaCl (salt). Remind them that salt (NaCl) is safe to eat even though sodium and chlorine alone are dangerous.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with gallery walk (Constructing explanations): learners must link observations and numbers to the mechanism (outer electrons), so the explanation is evidence-based rather than a memorised statement. Peer critique during the gallery walk sharpens reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for explanations that (a) state Cl has 7 outer electrons and is one short of a full shell; (b) state Ne (2,8) and Ar (2,8,8) have full outer shells so do not react; (c) use 0.5 mg/L to explain why only a small dose is used; (d) connect NaCl to the salt that is safe to eat. Use a 3-2-1 rubric: 3 = all four elements, 2 = two or three, 1 = one or none. Record names of learners with misconceptions for follow-up and plan a short re-teach with the electron arrangements on the board.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 10 min) Akinyi and Kiprop, the DQB keepers, lead the class to revisit the Driving Question Board. Learners (1) pick at least one earlier sticky note they can now answer (for example Kiprop's 'Why do street lamps glow yellow?' or 'Why is chlorine in our water?') and write the answer on the back citing evidence from this lesson; (2) write one new question on a new sticky note (for example 'Why does iron rust but gold does not?', 'Why is the sodium lamp yellow and the neon sign red?', 'Is chlorine in water safe for everyone?', 'Which element is best for a new sufuria?'); and (3) place each note under 'Properties', 'Reactivity', 'Uses' or 'Safety'. The class counts how many 'Reactivity' and 'Safety' questions are answered and agrees which questions the next lesson (transition metals) should tackle.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Akinyi, Kiprop, which questions on our wall can we now answer using chlorine and the noble gases?" Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 learners to read a note they answered and state the evidence used. Ask: "Which question can we NOT answer yet? What evidence would we need?" Redirect questions about transition metals, hardness and rusting to Lesson 7. Praise good questions that link position in the periodic table to a job. Keep the DQB visible and move answered notes into a 'Now we can explain' column.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (tracking growing understanding): linking old questions to new evidence shows learners their own progress, and new questions keep the inquiry going toward the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that (a) each learner posts one answer with evidence and one new question; (b) sorted notes are in the right category; (c) at least two questions are now marked answered (for example about the Mombasa water and the street lamp). Observe whether new questions move from 'what happens' to 'why it happens', and note learners still asking only descriptive questions.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 13 min) At the class wall periodic table (the Family Model), learners add this lesson's evidence. In groups they annotate Group 17 (F, Cl): '7 outer electrons, one short of a full shell, reactive non-metals; Cl is a greenish-yellow toxic gas used at about 0.5 mg/L to treat Mombasa and Nairobi water; 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl'. They annotate Group 18 (He, Ne, Ar): 'full outer shell (He 2, Ne 2,8, Ar 2,8,8), unreactive, gases with very low boiling points; Ne used in signs, Ar in lamps'. They then update the model's rule: 'Reactivity depends on outer electrons: Group 1 lose 1 easily (very reactive), Group 2 lose 2 (less reactive), Group 17 are one short of a full shell (reactive non-metals), Group 18 are full (unreactive).' Each learner draws a quick sketch of Na, Cl and Ne showing their outer electrons and adds a one-line note on the job each suits. They finish by completing the summary table (below) in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Our family model must predict, not just describe. Using the position of an element in the table, what can we predict?" Hand a marker to a different group for each annotation. WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups propose wording. Cold-call 4 learners to defend a line on the model with evidence. Ask: "How does the model now explain the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle? Which parts are still missing?" Point out that Lesson 7 will add transition metals (copper wire, iron and zinc for mabati) and Lesson 8 will use the whole model to choose the right element for a job. Check that every annotation uses 'outer electrons' (not 'valence electrons'), 'chemical family' and 'group', and that no ionic bonding detail has been added.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (Developing and using models): adding new evidence to the shared class periodic table and refining the rule linking outer electrons to reactivity and use turns separate facts into one predictive model that can be applied to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each learner's sketch shows Na 2,8,1, Cl 2,8,7 and Ne 2,8 correctly and that annotations on the model name the family, the number of outer electrons, the behaviour and one use. Exit check: ask 3 cold-called learners to state, in one sentence each, why chlorine is used in small doses and why neon suits signs. Collect the summary tables to gauge who needs support before Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners explain reactivity using outer electrons (Cl one short of a full shell; Ne and Ar already full) rather than saying 'chlorine is bad' or 'noble gases are lazy'? (2) Could they use the 0.5 mg/L data to explain why the dose matters and why a toxic gas can make water safe? (3) Did any learners think the sodium lamp contains neon, or that salt is dangerous because sodium and chlorine are? How did you address it? (4) Was the chlorine demonstration safe and well ventilated, or did you rely on the video, and what would you change? (5) Which DQB questions remain unanswered and how will Lesson 7 on transition metals address them? (6) Which learners need extra help balancing 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl or drawing electron arrangements, and what support will you provide?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Record what you observed about chlorine (colour, reaction with sodium, product NaCl), the water treatment data (about 0.5 mg/L of chlorine, 10 mg for 20 L), and the data for neon and argon (colourless gases, 2,8 and 2,8,8, boiling points -246 C and -186 C, unreactive, non-conductors).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Write what you learned: halogens (Group 17) have 7 outer electrons and are reactive non-metals; chlorine kills the bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid at a tiny dose, but is toxic in large amounts; noble gases (Group 18) have full outer shells (He 2, Ne 2,8, Ar 2,8,8) and are unreactive; the balanced equation 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Explain, using outer electrons, why Mombasa tap water treated with chlorine is safe for Mama Wanjiru's ugali, why sodium and chlorine make safe table salt together, and why unreactive noble gases such as neon suit signs and road lighting. State how this helps answer the driving question: how the periodic table helps us match an element to a job.

LESSONS.title: Transition Metals: Matching Properties to Jobs (Copper, Iron, Zinc, Lead and Aluminium)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: transition metals, copper, iron, zinc, lead, aluminium, density, melting point, conductivity, galvanising, sacrificial protection, trade-off, toxicity, mabati, sufuria

slo.purpose: To help learners use physical property data to explain why transition metals (and lead and aluminium for comparison) are chosen for particular jobs in Kenyan daily life, and to weigh trade-offs such as the toxicity of lead.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) locate the transition block on the periodic table (between Group 2 and Group 13, from Period 4) and state that Fe (Z=26), Cu (Z=29) and Zn (Z=30) are transition metals; (b) state that transition metals are generally strong, dense, good conductors with high melting points, using the data (Fe 7.87 g/cm3, 1538 C; Cu 8.96 g/cm3, 1085 C; Zn 7.14 g/cm3, 420 C); (c) outline the uses of Cu (electrical wire), Fe (structural steel and mabati base), Zn (galvanising coat that protects iron by sacrificial protection), Pb (car batteries and radiation shielding) and Al (sufuria); (d) explain why lead is being phased out despite its usefulness, because it is dense but toxic.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (matching table); analysing and interpreting data (comparing density, melting point and conductivity); obtaining, evaluating and communicating information from digital and print sources; constructing explanations and arguing from evidence (claim-evidence-reasoning for an element-to-job match); observing and comparing samples of Fe, Cu, Zn and Al safely.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the uses of elements of the periodic table in day-to-day life (KICD Sub-Strand 2.2); respect peers' opinions during discussion; take care of self and others by observing safety (Love); use digital devices responsibly (Responsibility). Core competencies: Digital literacy as the learner uses available digital and print media to research on transition elements and their uses. PCI: Safety and security (handling metal samples and lead information).
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 4 to 6 explained reactive families (alkali metals, magnesium, halogens and noble gases) using outer electrons. This lesson turns to the strong, dense metals we meet daily in the copper wire and the zinc-coated iron mabati of Lesson 1, and gives the class evidence that a job is matched to specific properties, with trade-offs. It builds on Lesson 2 (position of the transition block) and Lesson 3 (physical properties data), and prepares Lesson 8, where learners choose the right element for a new Kenyan product.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners may handle small samples of Fe, Cu, Zn and Al with goggles on; no sodium, potassium or lithium is handled by learners. Lead is NOT handled by learners; it is studied only through data, pictures and video because it is toxic. Wash hands after handling metal samples; do not put samples near the mouth; wear goggles; tell the teacher about cuts from sharp edges and use the first aid kit. Handle digital devices appropriately and follow the school's online safety rules.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru's aluminium sufuria, the copper wire in the kettle cable and the zinc-coated iron mabati from Kericho farm buildings are all metals, yet each does a different job. Learners predict which metal suits which job, then gather evidence by examining Fe, Cu, Zn and Al samples and a physical data table (Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Al), and by researching uses with print and digital sources. In the Explain phase they build claim-evidence-reasoning arguments matching property to use, including why zinc protects iron and why lead is dense but toxic so its use is being reduced. They then post new questions on the DQB and add the transition block and uses to the class family model, advancing the driving question of how the periodic table helps match element to job.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners look at four anchor objects or pictures from Lesson 1: the aluminium sufuria, the copper wire from a kettle cable, a piece of mabati (iron coated with zinc) and a picture of a car battery (lead). On a prediction sheet they individually write: (1) which property of each metal makes it right for its job, and (2) what they think would go wrong if the metals were swapped (e.g. a lead cooking pot, an aluminium mabati roof, a zinc electric wire). They then share with a partner and keep the sheet to revisit in the Explain phase.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the sufuria and say: "Mama Wanjiru in Mombasa cooks ugali in this. Why this metal and not the metal in the mabati roof? Write your prediction first, silently." Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before any talk and 2 minutes of silent writing. Then say: "Turn to your partner and compare. Do you agree on at least one property?" Cold-call 4 learners from different parts of the room, accepting all ideas without judging, and record keywords (strong, light, conducts, does not rust) on the board. Ask: "What would you want to see in the data to test that idea?" Point to the Lesson 2 wall periodic table and ask: "Where do Fe, Cu and Zn sit? Come and point." Invite 2 learners to show the block between Group 2 and Group 13 starting at Period 4. Remind them that this is the position taught in Lesson 2.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with elicitation of prior ideas: writing a prediction before seeing data makes learners commit to an initial model of 'property to job', so that later evidence can confirm or revise it. Linking the objects to the family model keeps the phenomenon (the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle) in view.
framework.formativeAssessment: Scan prediction sheets and look for: (a) at least one named property per metal (conductivity, strength, low mass, rust protection); (b) whether learners mention reactivity ideas from Lessons 4 to 6 inappropriately; (c) whether at least 3 learners can correctly point to the transition block. Tally common ideas (e.g. 'metals are all strong') on the board to revisit as misconceptions.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) In groups of 4, learners rotate through two stations for 10 minutes each, then spend 5 minutes on a research task. Station 1 (samples, goggles on): examine and compare small samples of Fe (nail), Cu (wire), Zn (strip or galvanised nail) and Al (offcut from a sufuria): colour, shine, how easily each bends, mass of equal-sized pieces by feel or balance, and whether each conducts using a simple cell, bulb and wires. They record results in a table. Station 2 (data): they study the physical data table for Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb and Al: density (Fe 7.87, Cu 8.96, Zn 7.14, Pb 11.34, Al 2.70 g/cm3), melting point (Fe 1538, Cu 1085, Zn 420, Pb 327, Al 660 C) and conductivity (Cu excellent; Fe, Zn, Al conduct; Pb poor-to-moderate). They answer: which is densest, which has the highest melting point, which has the lowest melting point among the five, and which is lightest. Research task: using print resources or a digital device (offline resources if no internet), each group finds the uses of one metal (Cu - wiring, Fe - steel and mabati base, Zn - galvanising, Pb - car batteries and radiation shielding, Al - sufuria) and notes one reason for the use.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the rotation say: "Goggles on. Samples are for looking, bending and testing only; nothing goes near your mouth. Lead is not in the box. We study it from data only because it is toxic." Circulate and ask: "Which sample felt heavier for the same size? What does the density table say?" and "What did the bulb do for each metal? Is that what the data says about Cu?" Pause with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to report the densest and the highest-melting metal. Ask: "Fe, Cu and Zn are all transition metals. What do they have in common in the data compared with Na and K from Lesson 3?" (higher density, higher melting point, harder; Na and K float, these sink). Prompt: "Aluminium is not in the transition block. Does it still fit a job? Why?" Assign each group one metal for the research task and give 5 minutes. Have first aid kit visible.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table analysis with pattern finding (Gallery of evidence): comparing hands-on observations with numerical data lets learners see patterns across metals (high density and melting points for transition metals; low density for Al; low melting point for Pb and Zn). Linking back to Lesson 3's method for comparing properties reinforces data-based reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that groups: (a) correctly record at least 3 observations per sample; (b) read the data table correctly, naming Pb as densest (11.34 g/cm3), Fe as highest melting (1538 C) and Pb as lowest melting among Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Al (327 C); (c) observe goggles and handling rules; (d) correctly pair each metal with its use and give one reason. Note groups that confuse density with strength or that claim all metals conduct equally.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Learners return to their predictions and write one claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) paragraph for the element-to-job match assigned by the teacher: (1) Cu for the kettle wire, (2) Fe for the mabati base and steel, (3) Zn for the coat on mabati, (4) Al for the sufuria, (5) Pb for car batteries. They use data: e.g. Cu has excellent conductivity and is ductile so can be drawn into wire; Al has low density (2.70 g/cm3), heats food quickly and resists corrosion through its oxide layer; Fe is strong and cheap but rusts, so it is coated with Zn, which is more reactive than iron and corrodes first (sacrificial protection), which links to Lesson 5's idea that more reactive metals lose electrons more readily and to the Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 reaction. For lead, groups discuss the trade-off: Pb is very dense (11.34 g/cm3), good for batteries and radiation shielding, but toxic, so its use is being reduced and never suits a cooking pot. Groups then hold a whole-class 'job interview': a learner reads a job (e.g. 'overhead cable in Nairobi', 'cooking pot for Gikomba jua kali artisans', 'roof in Kericho') and groups argue which metal to hire and why. Learners then revise their original predictions in a different colour.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one CER: "Claim: copper suits wire. Evidence: its conductivity is excellent and it is ductile. Reasoning: current must pass easily and the metal must be drawn into thin strands." Then give 4 minutes for groups to write their own. Ask: "Mama Wanjiru's pot is safe but she asks why chlorine gas is poisonous. For metals, what makes lead a poor choice for a pot even though it is soft and melts at 327 C?" Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: "If a mabati sheet is scratched, why does the iron underneath still not rust straight away?" Guide them to sacrificial protection: zinc is more reactive, so it is used up first. Use the sentence stem: "The metal is chosen because ____ (property), shown by ____ (data), but the trade-off is ____." Correct the misconception that all transition metals are equally good conductors by returning to the data table. During the job interview, cold-call 5 different groups and invite counter-arguments with: "Who can respectfully challenge that with a different data point?" Remind learners not to introduce bonding detail, since it is not part of this lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with structured argumentation: learners must link a property in the data to a job and name the trade-off, building the habit of justifying choices with evidence. The job interview applies the matching model to new contexts, showing why the periodic table and properties together help predict suitable elements.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for CER paragraphs that: (a) state a clear claim; (b) quote at least one correct number from the data (e.g. Al 2.70 g/cm3, Pb 11.34 g/cm3, Zn 420 C); (c) give a scientific reason; (d) name a trade-off such as lead toxicity, rusting of iron or cost. Use a 3-point check (claim, evidence, reasoning). Listen for correct use of 'sacrificial protection' and 'zinc more reactive than iron'. Note learners who suggest lead for cooking or copper as a roof without addressing cost.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min, shared with the end of Explain) Akinyi and Kiprop, the DQB keepers, lead the class in adding new questions on sticky notes (e.g. 'Why is copper cable so much more expensive than iron?', 'What happens to old car batteries in Nairobi?', 'Why is aluminium not a transition metal but still used for sufuria?'). Learners sort the notes under Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety, and move any earlier questions they can now answer (e.g. 'Why is the sufuria safe?', 'Why does mabati not rust quickly?') to an 'Answered' column with a short evidence note.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look back at our board from Lesson 1. Which question can we now answer with evidence from today?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to move a note and justify it with data. Ask each learner to write one new question on a sticky note and hand it to Akinyi or Kiprop to place. Say: "Which question needs evidence we do not have yet? That will help us in Lesson 8." Point out gaps (cost and availability) as items to weigh in Lesson 8. Praise respectful listening.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking: moving answered questions and posting new ones makes learning progress visible, links the lesson back to the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle and shows how the evidence advances the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count how many learners contribute a new question and whether notes are placed in the correct category. Check that at least 3 learners move a note to 'Answered' with a data-based reason. Look for questions that show curiosity about cost, safety or recycling, which signal readiness for Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners add to the class Family Model (wall periodic table): they mark the transition block (Sc to Zn, including Fe26, Cu29 and Zn30) and place labelled cards for Cu - wiring (excellent conductor, ductile), Fe - steel and mabati base (strong, cheap), Zn - galvanising (more reactive than iron, sacrificial protection), Al - sufuria (light, conducts heat, oxide layer), and Pb (Z=82, Group 14, a post-transition metal taught here as a heavy metal) - batteries and shielding (dense, toxic). In their notebooks they add a mini table: metal, key property with number, use, trade-off. They also add a line: 'Transition metals are strong, dense, good conductors with high melting points, so uses are matched to specific properties.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Come and place one card on the model and say aloud the property and the data that support it." Invite 5 learners (cold-call, different groups) and ask the class to agree or correct with a thumbs signal. Clarify: "Pb is in Group 14, not the transition block, and Al is in Group 13, but we compare them here for use." Ask: "How does the periodic table help predict which metal could do a job? What else besides position do we need?" (data on properties, safety, cost, availability). Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before each cold call. Close by connecting to the earlier families: "Reactive families like sodium are dangerous alone; these metals are chosen for strength, conduction and low reactivity." Preview Lesson 8: choosing the right element for a new Kenyan product.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding transition metals and their uses to the wall periodic table extends the class model from reactivity (Lessons 4 to 6) to properties and uses, helping learners see how position, properties and trade-offs combine to answer the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners place Fe, Cu and Zn in the transition block and correctly label Pb and Al as outside it. In notebooks, look for a complete mini table with one correct number, one use and one trade-off for each of 5 metals. Ask 3 learners to give a one-sentence answer to 'Why is copper used for wire and lead not used for pots?' and record accuracy.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners use numbers from the data table (not just general statements) in their CER paragraphs? (2) Did any learners confuse density with strength, or assume lead and aluminium are transition metals? (3) Was the sacrificial protection idea understood by linking to zinc's higher reactivity? (4) Did every learner participate safely with the metal samples and avoid contact with lead? (5) Which DQB questions about cost, recycling or availability should be addressed in Lesson 8? Note which learners need support with reading data tables or writing reasoning, and adjust groups. Check that offline print resources were sufficient where digital devices were limited.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We examined samples of Fe, Cu, Zn and Al and a data table for Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb and Al: density (Fe 7.87, Cu 8.96, Zn 7.14, Pb 11.34, Al 2.70 g/cm3), melting point (Fe 1538, Cu 1085, Zn 420, Pb 327, Al 660 C) and conductivity (Cu excellent). We also researched their uses: wiring, mabati, galvanising, batteries and sufuria.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Transition metals such as Fe, Cu and Zn are generally strong, dense, good conductors with high melting points, and each use matches a specific property. Fe is strong and cheap, Cu is an excellent conductor and ductile, Zn coats iron and protects it by sacrificial protection, Al is light and resists corrosion, and Pb is very dense but toxic so its use is being reduced.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Mama Wanjiru's sufuria is aluminium because it is light, conducts heat and resists corrosion; the kettle wire is copper because it conducts electricity excellently and can be drawn into wire; the mabati roof is iron for strength coated with zinc because zinc is more reactive and corrodes first. Elements are chosen for properties, balanced against trade-offs such as lead's toxicity, cost and availability.
