LESSONS.title: Putting It Together: Choosing the Right Element for the Job
LESSONS.aresKeywords: chemical families, periodic table position, outer electrons, reactivity, properties and uses, sodium, chlorine, aluminium, copper, zinc, noble gases, safety, final explanation

slo.purpose: Learners use evidence from properties, reactivity and periodic table position to justify choosing an element for a new Kenyan product, weighing safety, cost and availability, and complete the family model and the Driving Question Board.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify chemical families in the periodic table, b) classify elements of the periodic table into their chemical families, c) investigate the physical and chemical properties of selected elements of the periodic table, d) outline the uses of elements of the periodic table, e) appreciate the uses of the elements of the periodic table in day-to-day life. In this lesson learners link all of these: elements are chosen for jobs because of their properties, which depend on outer electrons and so on position in the periodic table. Sodium (2,8,1) reacts violently with water because its single outer electron is lost very easily, but combined with chlorine as NaCl it is stable and safe to eat. Chlorine kills microbes at about 0.5 mg/L in Mombasa water. Aluminium suits the sufuria, copper suits wire, zinc coats iron for mabati, and neon suits signs.
slo.skills: Science and Engineering Practices: constructing explanations and designing solutions (final explanation and product recommendation); engaging in argument from evidence (defending an element choice with a claim, evidence and reasoning); developing and using models (comparing the Lesson 1 model with the final family model); obtaining, evaluating and communicating information. Core competencies: Self-efficacy and Digital literacy (research and present transition metal uses), Critical thinking and problem solving.
slo.attitudes: Love: take care of self and others by observing safety when handling elements and appropriately using first aid kits in case of injuries. Respect: listen to and consider peers' arguments. Appreciate the uses of the elements of the periodic table in day-to-day life. PCI: Road safety (properties that make sodium suited to illuminating roads) and Safety and security.
slo.keyInquiry: How are elements suited to their use in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 8 is the culmination. Learners return to the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle from Lesson 1 and answer the Driving Question Board using the evidence from Lessons 1-7: families and layout (L2), physical property patterns (L3), alkali metal reactivity and outer electrons (L4), magnesium and reactivity order (L5), halogens and noble gases (L6) and transition metal uses and trade-offs (L7). They write a final explanation and recommend an element for a new Kenyan product.
slo.safetyNotes: No new reactive-metal practical is done in this lesson. If the sodium demonstration is replayed, only Mr. Otieno-style teacher demonstration behind a safety screen with goggles and lab coat, a pea-sized piece (about 0.1 g) only, sodium kept in paraffin oil, no water near stored sodium. Learners do not handle Na, K or Li. Learners may handle Mg ribbon, Al, Cu, Fe and Zn samples with goggles on. Keep the first aid kit visible. Remind learners that lead is toxic and samples must be handled with clean hands washed afterwards, and chlorine gas is never produced in class.

LESSONS.overview: In Lesson 1 learners met a puzzle: the aluminium sufuria, copper wire, mabati roof (iron coated with zinc), table salt, chlorinated Mombasa water and the Thika Road sodium lamp are all useful and safe, yet sodium reacts violently with water and chlorine gas is poisonous. Mama Wanjiru, a food seller in Mombasa, asked why her pot is safe while chlorine in her tap water is poisonous as a gas. In this final lesson learners predict which element they would choose for new products, revisit the evidence cards from Lessons 1-7, build a final explanation using claim-evidence-reasoning, complete the DQB by sorting answers under Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety, and compare their Lesson 1 initial model with the final class family model. They finish by recommending an element for a new Kenyan product, weighing properties, safety, cost and availability, and reflect on caring for self and others.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown a design challenge card: 'A jua kali artisan in Gikomba wants to make (a) a cooking pot, (b) a cable for a charger, (c) a roof sheet for a farm store in Kericho. Which element would you pick for each: sodium, aluminium, copper, iron coated with zinc, or neon?' Individually, in 3 minutes, learners write a prediction and one reason for each, using only what they already know. They then also predict: 'Which of these elements could we NOT use on its own, and why?' They record predictions in their science notebooks to compare with the final explanation later.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the six anchor objects (sufuria, copper wire, mabati, salt, a bottle of treated water, picture of the Thika Road lamp) and the challenge card. Say: 'Remember Mama Wanjiru's question? Before we revisit our evidence, write what you think. There are no wrong predictions today.' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after posing each question before anyone speaks. Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) to share one choice and one reason; ask a fifth: 'Who disagrees with that choice and why?' Record two competing predictions on the board without judging. Ask: 'Which prediction would you most like us to test with evidence?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas through individual written prediction then cold-call sharing. Writing predictions before revisiting evidence makes learners' initial thinking visible, creates cognitive conflict between peers' choices, and gives a baseline to compare with their final explanation, so they see their own learning growth.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (1) name properties such as light, conductive or unreactive in their reasons, (2) mention safety for sodium, (3) refer to the periodic table or outer electrons. Tally on a checklist: how many give property-only reasons, how many mention family or outer electrons, how many choose sodium for a pot. Use the tally to decide which evidence card to emphasise in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners do an evidence gallery review. Each group receives a set of data cards drawn from the lesson sequence: (1) Physical data table: Na density 0.97 g/cm3, melting 98 C, soft; Al 2.70 g/cm3, melting 660 C; Cu 8.96 g/cm3, melting 1085 C, excellent conductor; Fe 7.87 g/cm3, melting 1538 C; Zn 7.14 g/cm3, melting 420 C; Pb 11.34 g/cm3, melting 327 C, toxic; Ne boils at -246 C, Ar at -186 C. (2) Reactivity order K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg with 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 and 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. (3) Electron arrangements: Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Cl 2,8,7; Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8. (4) Chlorine data: greenish-yellow gas, 0.5 mg/L in Mombasa water, 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl. (5) Uses list: Cu wire, Fe structural steel and mabati base, Zn galvanising by sacrificial protection, Pb batteries but toxic, Al sufuria with oxide layer. Learners also handle real samples (Mg ribbon, Al, Cu, Fe, Zn) with goggles on and compare appearance and feel. Each group fills an Element Job Matrix with columns: element, family and position, outer electrons, key property, safe use, trade-off. They also locate each element on the wall family model.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your job is to become the evidence experts. Every claim you make today must be backed by a card.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which card tells you why sodium cannot be a sufuria? Show me.' and 'What does the 2,8,1 arrangement tell you about how sodium behaves?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before prompting. Check goggles are on when samples are handled. Cold-call 3 groups to report one row of their matrix. Prompt: 'Where does Al sit compared with the four families we studied? What does that tell us about naming it a transition metal or not?' (Al is an other metal, not in the four families.) Correct misconceptions: salt (NaCl) is a compound and is not the same as sodium; chlorine gas and chlorine in 0.5 mg/L water are the same element at very different doses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-card gallery with an Element Job Matrix (data organisation and pattern finding). Structuring data in one table across families lets learners see that properties come from outer electrons and position, and that safety depends on whether an element is free or combined and on dose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each matrix for: correct family for Na, Mg, Cl, Ne, Cu, Zn; correct outer electrons (Na 1, Mg 2, Cl 7, Ne 8); a property tied to a use for each of Al, Cu, Fe, Zn; at least one trade-off (Pb toxic, Na reactive). Success indicator: 80% of groups complete 5 rows correctly. Note groups who put Al in a family or confuse NaCl with Na for reteaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write the Final Explanation individually using a claim-evidence-reasoning frame to answer the Driving Question and Mama Wanjiru's question: 'Why is sodium dangerous alone but salt safe, why is chlorine poisonous as a gas but safe in Mombasa water, and why is each element chosen for its job?' Frame: Claim (an element is chosen for its job because...), Evidence (at least three data points from cards, e.g. Na 2,8,1 loses its outer electron easily, 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; 0.5 mg/L chlorine kills cholera and typhoid bacteria; Al is light 2.70 g/cm3 with an oxide layer; Cu excellent conductor), Reasoning (links to outer electrons and periodic table position, and to safety, cost, availability). Then pairs swap and use a checklist to give one star and one wish. Next, groups design a new product recommendation: choose one scenario (water pipe for a Kisumu school, cooking pot for Gikomba jua kali, electric cable, bright sign for a Nairobi shop, roofing for a Kericho tea store) and argue for an element, rejecting at least one alternative with evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first sentence of the frame: 'Sodium is unsuitable for a sufuria because its one outer electron is lost very easily, so it reacts violently with water.' Then say: 'Now it is your turn. Use at least three pieces of evidence and one trade-off.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each prompt. Questions to push reasoning: 'Why does combining with chlorine make sodium safe?' (the sodium atom has lost its outer electron and the compound NaCl is stable; do not go into ionic bonding detail.) 'If copper is such a good conductor, why not use it for the sufuria?' (cost, availability; Al is light and cheaper.) 'Why do we put zinc on iron?' (sacrificial protection). Cold-call 5 learners to read their reasoning sentence aloud and ask peers to name the evidence used. For each group's product pitch, ask: 'What is the safety risk and what is the cost trade-off?' Allow 90 seconds per group pitch and have two groups challenge each pitch.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning argumentation with peer critique. Requiring each claim to be tied to data and to atomic structure builds an explanation that links the macroscopic uses with the particle-level cause, and the product-pitch design task transfers the explanation to a new Kenyan context, which tests true understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Rubric on the final explanation (4 levels): Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below. Meets requires a correct claim, three data points, reasoning linking outer electrons or position to behaviour, and one safety or cost trade-off. Observe whether learners distinguish element from compound, and free chlorine gas from a 0.5 mg/L dose. Collect explanations; target feedback on those who cite uses without referring to outer electrons or periodic table position.

framework.learnerExperience: Akinyi and Kiprop lead the class back to the Driving Question Board with sticky notes sorted into Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety. Each group takes 4 original questions from Lesson 1, such as Akinyi's 'Why is sodium dangerous?' and Kiprop's 'Why do street lamps glow yellow?', and writes an answer on a new coloured note using evidence and the lesson where it was learned. Learners mark each question Answered, Partly answered or New question. They add at least one new question for further inquiry, for example 'Why do other metals give different flame colours?' or 'How is lead replaced in batteries?'. The class counts how many questions moved from open to answered in each category.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Akinyi and Kiprop, read your first questions aloud. Who can answer one with evidence?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to place an answer note and justify it with a card. Ask: 'Which question can we only partly answer? What evidence would we need?' Ensure each category has at least two answers. Redirect off-topic or incorrect answers by asking 'Which evidence card supports that?' Remind: the Thika Road lamp glows yellow because of sodium vapour in the lamp, which links to sodium's properties as an element; do not claim more than the lessons taught. Praise new questions as part of science.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board revisit and categorisation. Moving questions from open to answered shows learners the progress of the whole class, makes the link between the phenomenon and each lesson explicit, and validates unanswered questions as the start of future inquiry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each answer note cites evidence and a lesson, correctly sits under its category, and that Safety answers mention goggles, small quantities, no bare hands, or dose. Count the share of original questions answered (target: at least 80%). Note which questions stay partly answered and carry them forward as follow-up topics.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners compare their Lesson 1 initial model (a drawing or list of why objects are useful) with the completed class family model, a large wall periodic table annotated each lesson. In groups they produce a final model poster: a periodic table sketch showing the alkali metals (Na 2,8,1 with a 1 outer electron label), alkaline earth metals (Mg 2,8,2), halogens (Cl 2,8,7), noble gases (Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8) and the transition block (Fe, Cu, Zn), with Al and Pb noted, and arrows from each element to its Kenyan use (sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, Mombasa water, Thika Road lamp, neon signs). Each poster includes a Prediction Rule: 'The position in the periodic table tells us the number of outer electrons, which predicts reactivity and use.' Then learners complete a Then and Now comparison: what did my first model leave out, and what did I add? They end with a short safety and care reflection: one rule that protects self and others and how they would help a classmate with an injury using the first aid kit.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Place your Lesson 1 model next to your final model. What changed?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to point to one added idea and the evidence behind it. Ask: 'Using only the periodic table, predict whether potassium would be a good sufuria, and why not.' (K is in Group 1, reactive, more than Na; reactivity K > Na > Li.) 'What would you predict for a Group 17 element above chlorine in a similar role?' only if time allows, otherwise skip. Check posters show correct outer electrons and that Na, Cl and NaCl are not confused. Close with: 'Return to Mama Wanjiru: how would you explain to her why her pot and her tap water are safe?' Select 2 learners to answer in under 30 seconds each.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model comparison (Lesson 1 vs final) with a Prediction Rule. Putting the first and final models side by side makes conceptual change visible, and writing a rule that links position, outer electrons, reactivity and use gives learners a transferable tool for predicting unfamiliar elements.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that (1) place all five families correctly, (2) link outer electron number to reactivity, (3) connect every anchor object to an element and property, (4) mention safety, cost or availability. Use a 4-point checklist per group. Exit ticket: 'Write one new element job match and defend it in two sentences.' Learners who cannot link position to behaviour get a quick one-to-one with the family table.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did learners explain sodium's danger and salt's safety using outer electrons rather than just saying 'it changes'? Could they separate free chlorine gas from a 0.5 mg/L dose? How many used the periodic table position as a reason, not just a list of uses? FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: General Science Grade 10: 2.2 Chemical Families – Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation for the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle. Remember Mama Wanjiru, the food seller in Mombasa, who asked why her aluminium sufuria is safe while chlorine in her tap water is poisonous as a gas. Use the evidence you collected in Lessons 1 to 8, the class family model and the Driving Question Board (DQB) to answer each question in the space below it. Write in full sentences. For each answer, use a claim (what you think), evidence (data or observations from our lessons) and reasoning (the idea of outer electrons and position in the periodic table that links them). Use the words element, compound, group, period and chemical family correctly. Write balanced equations with -> where asked. Use these data when you need them. Sodium (Na): density 0.97 g/cm3, melting point 98 C. Magnesium (Mg): density 1.74 g/cm3, melting point 650 C. Aluminium (Al): density 2.70 g/cm3, melting point 660 C. Copper (Cu): density 8.96 g/cm3, melting point 1085 C, excellent conductor. Lead (Pb): density 11.34 g/cm3, melting point 327 C. Water has a density of 1.00 g/cm3. Chlorine is added to Mombasa water at about 0.5 mg/L.

sections.title: Part 1: Why is sodium dangerous alone?
sections.prompt: In the demonstration, Mr. Otieno dropped a pea-sized piece of sodium into water behind a safety screen. (a) Describe what you saw and what the pink colour with phenolphthalein showed. (b) Which chemical family does sodium belong to, and how many outer electrons does each atom have? Write its electron arrangement. (c) Explain why sodium reacts so violently with water. (d) Write the balanced equation for the reaction. (e) Lithium, sodium and potassium are in the same group. Explain how their reactivity compares and why.
sections.exemplar: (a) The sodium floated, fizzed, darted about and melted into a ball. The solution turned pink with phenolphthalein, which showed that an alkali (sodium hydroxide, NaOH) formed. (b) Sodium is an alkali metal (Group 1). Each atom has 1 outer electron. Its electron arrangement is 2,8,1. (c) Claim: Sodium is violent because its single outer electron is lost very easily. Evidence: it reacts fast in cold water, gives off hydrogen gas and melts. Reasoning: an atom that loses its outer electron easily reacts readily, so sodium is dangerous on its own and must be stored under paraffin oil and handled only by the teacher. (d) 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. (e) Reactivity increases down the group: Li < Na < K. Lithium fizzed slowly, sodium fast, and potassium very fast with a lilac flame. Down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases.

sections.title: Part 2: Sodium, chlorine and safe salt, and chlorine in Mombasa water
sections.prompt: Mama Wanjiru asks why chlorine in her tap water is safe when chlorine as a gas is poisonous, and why the sodium that is dangerous alone is in the salt she puts in her food. (a) Which chemical family is chlorine in, and how many outer electrons does it have? Write its electron arrangement. (b) Write the balanced equation for sodium reacting with chlorine. (c) Use the idea of outer electrons and what you know about the dose to explain to Mama Wanjiru why the tap water is safe. (d) Use outer electrons to explain why table salt is safe to eat even though sodium alone is dangerous.
sections.exemplar: (a) Chlorine is a halogen (Group 17). It has 7 outer electrons. Its electron arrangement is 2,8,7. It is a reactive non-metal. (b) 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl. (c) Claim: the water is safe because only a tiny dose is used. Evidence: chlorine is added at about 0.5 mg/L at the Mombasa water works, which means only 10 mg in 20 L of water, and at this dose it kills the bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid. Reasoning: a chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons and needs just one more, so it reacts readily, which is why it is good at killing microbes. Because it is so reactive it is toxic in large amounts, so only a small safe dose is used. (d) Sodium has 1 outer electron that it loses very easily, and chlorine needs one more outer electron to have 8. When they react, the outer electron of sodium is taken up by chlorine and they form the compound sodium chloride (NaCl), which is stable and has completely different properties from its elements. Sodium no longer has its easily lost outer electron to react violently with water, and chlorine is no longer a reactive poisonous gas, because both are combined in the stable compound, so the salt is safe to eat.

sections.title: Part 3: Reactivity and position in the periodic table
sections.prompt: Akinyi asked, 'If sodium is so dangerous, are all metals like that?' (a) Describe what happened when you tested magnesium ribbon in cold water, in dilute HCl and in air. (b) Compare magnesium with sodium using their electron arrangements and the evidence. (c) Write the balanced equations for magnesium burning in air and for magnesium reacting with dilute HCl. (d) Neon and argon do not react at all. Using outer electrons, explain why, and state a use that depends on this.
sections.exemplar: (a) Magnesium showed no visible reaction in cold water. It gave steady bubbles of hydrogen gas in dilute HCl (the pop test was positive). It burned with a bright white flame in air, leaving white MgO powder. (b) Sodium is 2,8,1 (1 outer electron) and magnesium is 2,8,2 (2 outer electrons, an alkaline earth metal in Group 2). Magnesium has to lose 2 outer electrons rather than 1, so it loses them less readily than sodium does. This matches the evidence: magnesium shows no reaction in cold water, whereas sodium fizzes fast and melts. So magnesium is less reactive than sodium, and the reactivity order is K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg. So not all metals are as dangerous as sodium. Position in the periodic table helps us predict this: Group 2 is less reactive than Group 1. (c) 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. (d) Noble gases (Group 18) have full outer shells (Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8), so their atoms do not need to lose or gain electrons and they are unreactive. Because neon is unreactive, it suits signs.

sections.title: Part 4: Matching metals to jobs
sections.prompt: Use the data given in the instructions and what you learned about the metals in the puzzle. (a) Using the data, give reasons why aluminium is used for Mama Wanjiru's sufuria. (b) Why is copper used for the wire in a kettle or jiko cable? (c) Why is the mabati roof made of iron coated with zinc? (d) Lead is the densest metal in the data but its use is being reduced. Explain why, using what you learned. (e) Compare sodium with aluminium using the data and explain why sodium would not suit a sufuria.
sections.exemplar: (a) Aluminium is light (2.70 g/cm3, much less dense than copper at 8.96 g/cm3), so the pot is easy to carry. It is a metal that conducts, so heat from the fire passes through it to the food, and it melts at 660 C, well above cooking temperatures, so it stays solid on the fire. It also resists corrosion because of its protective oxide layer, so it stays in good condition and is safe for cooking, unlike sodium. (b) Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity and can be drawn into wire (ductile). (c) Iron is strong and cheap, so it forms the base of the mabati. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first and protects the iron from rusting (sacrificial protection). (d) Lead is very dense (11.34 g/cm3) and is used in car batteries and radiation shielding, but it is toxic, so its use is being reduced. This shows that elements are chosen for their properties but with trade-offs such as safety. (e) Sodium is less dense than water (0.97 g/cm3 compared with 1.00 g/cm3) so it floats, and it melts at only 98 C, while aluminium melts at 660 C. Sodium also reacts violently with water. A sodium pot would melt on a fire and be dangerous, so aluminium is the better choice.

sections.title: Part 5: Answering the driving question
sections.prompt: Driving question: Why does each element behave and get used the way it does, and how can the periodic table help us predict which element is right for which job in Kenyan daily life? (a) Write a final explanation of the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle using claim, evidence and reasoning. Include outer electrons and position in the periodic table. (b) A jua kali artisan in Gikomba wants to make a new product: a cooking pot, a cable or a roof sheet. Choose one product, recommend an element and justify your choice using properties, safety, cost and availability. (c) How has your thinking changed since your first model in Lesson 1?
sections.exemplar: (a) Claim: Each element is used for a job because of its properties, which depend on its outer electrons and so on its position in the periodic table. Evidence: sodium (Group 1, 1 outer electron) reacts violently with water, but as NaCl it is stable and safe to eat. Chlorine (Group 17, 7 outer electrons) is a toxic gas in large amounts but kills microbes at about 0.5 mg/L in Mombasa water. Aluminium is light and conducts heat, so it suits the sufuria. Copper is an excellent conductor, so it suits wire. Zinc coats iron on mabati. Neon (full outer shell) is unreactive, so it suits signs, and sodium vapour gives the yellow-orange light of the Thika Road lamps. Reasoning: the periodic table lets us predict family behaviour, such as reactivity rising down Group 1, and so match element to job while balancing safety, cost and availability. (b) For a roof sheet I would recommend iron coated with zinc (galvanised mabati). Iron is strong and cheap, and zinc protects it from rusting. Both are available to Gikomba artisans, and the metals are safe to handle, unlike lead, which is toxic. (c) At first I thought each element is simply used for what it is good at, and I could not explain why sodium is dangerous but salt is safe. Now I can explain with outer electrons and position in the periodic table that reactivity and properties differ between families, and that compounds have different properties from their elements.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Why does each element behave and get used the way it does, and how can the periodic table help us predict which element is right for which job in Kenyan daily life?

lessons.title: The Sufuria, Wire, Mabati, Salt, Chlorine and Sodium-Lamp Puzzle
lessons.observed: We observed that everyday Kenyan objects are made from different elements: aluminium sufuria, copper wire, iron mabati coated with zinc, salt (NaCl), chlorine-treated Mombasa water and sodium-lamp light on Thika Road. We also saw sodium float, fizz, dart about and melt in water, and turn the solution pink with phenolphthalein.
lessons.learned: We learned that elements have very different properties, and some, like sodium, are dangerous on their own, yet each is useful and chosen for a job. We now have many questions about why an element suits a job, recorded on the DQB under Properties, Reactivity, Uses and Safety.
lessons.explained: Our first explanation is that each element is used for the job that its properties suit, but we cannot yet explain why sodium is violent alone yet safe in salt, or why chlorine is poisonous as a gas yet safe in tiny amounts in water. We will use the periodic table and later investigations to answer these questions.

lessons.title: Chemical Families: Sorting the First Twenty Elements by Position in the Periodic Table
lessons.observed: We sorted the first twenty elements by position on the periodic table. Li, Na and K are in Group 1 (alkali metals); Be, Mg and Ca are in Group 2 (alkaline earth metals); F and Cl are in Group 17 (halogens); He, Ne and Ar are in Group 18 (noble gases). H, B, C, N, O, Al, Si, P and S are not in any of these four families. The transition metals, including Fe, Cu and Zn, sit in the central block starting from Period 4.
lessons.learned: Elements are grouped into chemical families by their position in the periodic table. Groups are vertical columns and periods are horizontal rows. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons (Group 1 = 1, Group 2 = 2, Group 17 = 7, Group 18 = 8, with He = 2), which links group number to similar behaviour.
lessons.explained: Sodium (Na, Thika Road lamp and salt) is an alkali metal, chlorine (Cl, Mombasa water) is a halogen, aluminium (sufuria) is a metal not in the four families, and copper (wire), iron and zinc (mabati) are transition metals. So the elements in our puzzle come from different parts of the periodic table, and a family's position can help us predict behaviour. We still need evidence on their properties and reactivity to explain why each element suits its job.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of the Families: Finding Patterns in Density, Melting Point, Hardness and Conductivity
lessons.observed: We tested Mg, Al, Cu, Fe and Zn for appearance, hardness, density and conductivity, and studied a data table for Na, K, Li, Mg, Ca, Fe, Cu, Zn, Al, Pb, Cl2, Ne and Ar. Na, K and Li are soft with densities below water (0.97, 0.86, 0.53 g/cm3) and low melting points (98, 63, 181 C). Mg, Ca, Fe, Cu and Zn are denser and melt at higher temperatures. The metals conduct electricity; Cl2, Ne and Ar do not.
lessons.learned: Elements in the same chemical family share similar physical properties, and families differ from each other. Alkali metals are soft, low in density and low melting. Transition metals are hard, dense, high melting and good conductors. Position in the periodic table helps us predict physical properties, though there are exceptions such as soft, dense lead.
lessons.explained: Properties help explain why an element suits a job: aluminium is light and conducts heat for the sufuria, copper conducts electricity excellently for wire, and iron is strong for the mabati base. Sodium is soft, melts at only 98 C and floats, which helps us understand why it behaves differently from the metals we use for pots and wires. We still need to explain why the families differ and why sodium reacts so strongly with water, which we will investigate in Lesson 4.

lessons.title: Alkali Metals: Why One Outer Electron Makes Sodium Dangerous Alone but Safe in Salt
lessons.observed: Lithium fizzes slowly in water, sodium fizzes fast, melts into a ball and darts about, and potassium reacts very fast with a lilac flame. All three float and the solution turns pink with phenolphthalein. Freshly cut sodium is shiny but quickly dulls in air. (Record what you saw and heard in your own words.)
lessons.learned: Alkali metals (Group 1) have one outer electron (Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1). Reactivity increases down the group: Li < Na < K. They react with water to form an alkali (hydroxide) and hydrogen gas, and with oxygen in air. They must be stored under paraffin oil, handled only by the teacher, and any contact with skin or eyes needs immediate flushing with running water.
lessons.explained: Alkali metals are very reactive because each atom has a single outer electron that is lost very easily. Down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases. This is why sodium reacts violently with water (2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2) and is dangerous alone, which links to the sufuria, wire, mabati, salt, chlorine and sodium-lamp puzzle. We still need to explain why sodium combined as salt is safe.

lessons.title: Alkaline Earth Metals: Is Magnesium as Dangerous as Sodium?
lessons.observed: Magnesium ribbon showed no visible reaction in cold water, gave steady bubbles of hydrogen gas in dilute HCl (pop test positive), and burned with a bright white flame in air leaving white MgO powder. Sodium, by comparison, fizzes fast in water and melts.
lessons.learned: Alkaline earth metals (Group 2) have two outer electrons (Mg 2,8,2). Magnesium is less reactive than sodium. The reactivity order is K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg. Equations are balanced by adjusting coefficients so atoms are conserved.
lessons.explained: Both sodium and magnesium react by losing outer electrons, but magnesium reacts less readily, shown by no cold-water reaction and slower reaction with acid. Its position in the periodic table lets us predict this: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO and Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. So reactivity helps decide which element suits which job and how safely it can be handled.

lessons.title: Halogens and Noble Gases: Why Chlorine Cleans Mombasa Water and Neon Lights the Sign
lessons.observed: Record what you observed about chlorine (colour, reaction with sodium, product NaCl), the water treatment data (about 0.5 mg/L of chlorine, 10 mg for 20 L), and the data for neon and argon (colourless gases, 2,8 and 2,8,8, boiling points -246 C and -186 C, unreactive, non-conductors).
lessons.learned: Write what you learned: halogens (Group 17) have 7 outer electrons and are reactive non-metals; chlorine kills the bacteria that cause cholera and typhoid at a tiny dose, but is toxic in large amounts; noble gases (Group 18) have full outer shells (He 2, Ne 2,8, Ar 2,8,8) and are unreactive; the balanced equation 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl.
lessons.explained: Explain, using outer electrons, why Mombasa tap water treated with chlorine is safe for Mama Wanjiru's ugali, why sodium and chlorine make safe table salt together, and why unreactive noble gases such as neon suit signs and road lighting. State how this helps answer the driving question: how the periodic table helps us match an element to a job.

lessons.title: Transition Metals: Matching Properties to Jobs (Copper, Iron, Zinc, Lead and Aluminium)
lessons.observed: We examined samples of Fe, Cu, Zn and Al and a data table for Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb and Al: density (Fe 7.87, Cu 8.96, Zn 7.14, Pb 11.34, Al 2.70 g/cm3), melting point (Fe 1538, Cu 1085, Zn 420, Pb 327, Al 660 C) and conductivity (Cu excellent). We also researched their uses: wiring, mabati, galvanising, batteries and sufuria.
lessons.learned: Transition metals such as Fe, Cu and Zn are generally strong, dense, good conductors with high melting points, and each use matches a specific property. Fe is strong and cheap, Cu is an excellent conductor and ductile, Zn coats iron and protects it by sacrificial protection, Al is light and resists corrosion, and Pb is very dense but toxic so its use is being reduced.
lessons.explained: Mama Wanjiru's sufuria is aluminium because it is light, conducts heat and resists corrosion; the kettle wire is copper because it conducts electricity excellently and can be drawn into wire; the mabati roof is iron for strength coated with zinc because zinc is more reactive and corrodes first. Elements are chosen for properties, balanced against trade-offs such as lead's toxicity, cost and availability.

We learned that transition metals are strong, dense conductors, and that safety, cost and availability also affect which element is chosen.
